druid.summary: If the players on either side of the Druid share an alignment, the Demon can only attack them.
druid.examples:
On the second night, the Druid's 2 alive neighbours are the Baron (evil) and the Fortune Teller (good), so the Demon can attack anyone. That night the Demon kills the Saint.

On the second night, the Druid's 2 alive neighbours are the Saint (good) and the Fortune Teller (good). When waking the Demon, the Storyteller shows them the Druid's character token and points to the Saint player and the Fortune Teller player: the Demon can only choose them. That night the Demon kills the Saint.
druid.tips:
If you are the Druid, it is best not to reveal your character before the Demon's first attack, because you need that night's deaths to judge whether your ability worked. If the Demon knows you are the Druid, they may kill a player next to you on purpose to confuse you.

If you are the Druid and your 2 neighbours are the same alignment, the Demon can't kill you, or anyone other than those 2 players.

If you are the Druid and your ability worked, the Demon certainly knows you are the Druid by now. So if a player next to you dies at night, you had better reveal that you are the Druid and discuss last night's deaths with everyone.

If you are the Druid and a player next to you died at night because your ability forced the Demon to kill them, then your 2 neighbours share an alignment: either both good or both evil.

If you are the Demon and you are woken and told you can only choose 2 players, the player between them is certainly the Druid.

If you are the Demon, you know who the Druid is, and an evil player sits next to them, you can deliberately kill the good neighbour to make the evil one look good.

If you are the Demon: the Druid badly constrains your kills. Deal with them quickly, whether by execution or with a Minion's ability.

If you are the Demon and you find out the Druid is poisoned, their ability won't work, and the Druid will usually assume an evil player is sitting next to them. Use this to accuse the Druid's neighbours of being evil.
druid.bluffing:
Bluffing the Druid usually needs close coordination with the Demon; otherwise your story is hard to keep straight.

If you want to bluff the Druid, plan your strategy. A Druid usually comes forward when the night's death is not one of their alive neighbours, because that means an evil player sits next to them.

witness.ability: Each day, you may learn a true piece of info about 1 character type from the Storyteller. If the number of players of that type is abnormal, you learn false info instead.
witness.summary: Each day, the Witness learns something about a character type.
witness.examples:
A 12-player game (7/2/2/1), first day. The Witness visits the Storyteller and learns "The Fortune Teller and the Seamstress are both in play". Both are Townsfolk. In this game the Fang Gu added an Outsider and removed a Townsfolk, so there are 6 Townsfolk: the Townsfolk count is abnormal, and in fact the Fortune Teller and the Seamstress are not both in play. "The Fortune Teller and the Seamstress are both in play" is false information.

A 12-player game (7/2/2/1), third day. The Witness visits the Storyteller and learns "Alice is the Imp". The Imp is a Demon; the Demon in this game is the Imp, and there is a dead Imp and an alive Imp, so there are 2 Demons: the Demon count is abnormal, and in fact Alice is not the Demon. "Alice is the Imp" is false information.

A 12-player game (7/2/2/1), second day. The Witness visits the Storyteller and learns "The Baron is Alice or Bob". The Baron is a Minion; there are 2 Minions, which is normal, and Bob is the Baron. "The Baron is Alice or Bob" is true information.
witness.tips:
If you are the Witness, your information isn't necessarily true. Always remember: if the number of players of the character type you learn about is abnormal, your information is false! If you already know that a character who adds or removes Outsiders or Townsfolk is in play, you can deduce that your information about Outsiders or Townsfolk is false!

If you are the Witness, false information isn't useless either. If you can be sure a piece of information is false, the number of players of that character type is most likely abnormal, and you can reason from the reverse of that information.

If you are the Demon, the wealth of information the Witness brings is very bad for evil. Watch which players visit the Storyteller every day, pick out the Witness among them, and deal with them quickly.

If you are evil: whether the Witness's information is true depends on abnormal character counts. If the count of some character type in play is abnormal and good doesn't know it, mislead them as much as you can!

If you are evil and your ability can change character types, you can use it to make the Witness get false information.
witness.bluffing:
If you want to bluff the Witness, remember to visit the Storyteller every day, as if you were using the Witness's ability!

Be very careful! The Witness's information only ever involves one character type. If your information doesn't fit that format, you have all but admitted to being evil.

If you don't know what information to make up, ask the Storyteller for help! They will give you some useful suggestions.

Your information needs to tie in with "abnormal character counts" and should hold together logically; otherwise you may be called out as an evil player inventing information.

riddler.ability: Each day, you may learn a riddle from the Storyteller. Its answer is an in-play character.
riddler.summary: Each day, the Riddler gets a maddening riddle.
riddler.examples:
On the first day, the Riddler visits the Storyteller and learns "I heard your cold heartbeat". The answer is the Engineer, because the Engineer listens to machines at work.

On the first day, the Riddler visits the Storyteller and learns "Jinhua ham". The answer is the Sailor, because splitting "水手" (Sailor) into its characters and taking their opposites — water → fire, hand → leg — gives "火腿" (ham). [A Chinese wordplay riddle.]

On the first day, the Riddler visits the Storyteller and learns "6". The answer is the Gambler, because a die has 6 faces.

On the first day, the Riddler visits the Storyteller and learns "4". The answer is the Professor, because the Professor's icon has 4 atoms.

On the first day, the Riddler visits the Storyteller and learns "5". The answer is the Balloonist, because the Balloonist's Chinese name, 气球驾驶员, has 5 characters.

On the first day, the Riddler visits the Storyteller and learns "Crazy Thursday" (a fried-chicken promotion in China). The answer is the Pacifist, because the Pacifist's icon is a bird (hinting at chicken).

On the first day, the Riddler visits the Storyteller and learns "a great tonic" (as chicken soup is said to be). The answer is the Pacifist, because the Pacifist's icon is a bird (hinting at chicken).

On the first day, the Riddler visits the Storyteller and learns "Born to lie in pairs; open its mouth and it splits mountains and rivers". The answer is the Seamstress (scissors).
riddler.tips:
If you are the Riddler, do your best to work out which in-play character your riddle points to! If you really can't, publish your riddle and ask everyone for help.

If you are the Riddler and you really can't solve a riddle, use elimination: rule out characters it certainly isn't.

If you are evil: the Riddler can be very weak or very strong. Mislead everyone's guesses at the answers as much as you can, so that they misjudge which characters are in play!
riddler.bluffing:
If you are an evil player who doesn't fear death, make up any riddle you like! A number, a baffling sentence, even a gesture! You don't even need an answer! Who cares — let good puzzle over it!

If you are the Demon and bluffing the Riddler, be more careful when designing your riddles. Don't let people think you are just making things up: at least one or two riddles should clearly point to one or two in-play characters, so that you are more believable.

pearl_diver.ability: You start knowing how many steps you are from an evil player.
pearl_diver.summary: The Pearl Diver learns how far she is from an evil player.
pearl_diver.examples:
The Pearl Diver, player 1, learns "1", because she sits next to player 2, a Minion.

A 12-player game. The Pearl Diver, player 1, learns "5", because she is 5 steps from player 6, the Demon (clockwise).

A 12-player game. The Pearl Diver, player 1, learns "7", because she is 7 steps from player 6, the Demon (anticlockwise).

Player 1 is the Pearl Diver, player 2 a Minion, player 3 an Outsider and player 4 a Minion. The Pearl Diver learns "3": the player her information refers to is player 4.
pearl_diver.tips:
If you are the Pearl Diver and you learn 1, at least one of your 2 neighbours is evil! Make this public and try to execute them.

If you are the Pearl Diver, you can think of your ability simply as: you learn 2 players, at least one of whom is evil.

If you are the Pearl Diver and for some reason you believe your information is false (say the Vortox is in play), both players at the distance you learned are good.
pearl_diver.bluffing:
If you bluff the Pearl Diver, you can report a distance that lands on 2 good players, and so accuse them of including an evil player.

If you bluff the Pearl Diver and would rather survive, report a distance that really does include an evil player — a Minion, say. This makes it easier for everyone to trust that you are a real Pearl Diver.

paladin.ability: Each night, you learn 2 players: either neither is a Minion, or neither is the Demon. The 2 kinds of clue alternate each night.
paladin.summary: The Paladin learns which players are not Minions or not the Demon.
paladin.examples:
On the first night, the Paladin learns Alice and Bob: Alice is a Minion and Bob is a Townsfolk. On the second night, the Paladin learns Carol and Dave: Carol is the Demon and Dave is an Outsider. On the third night, the Paladin learns Dave and Bob: Dave is an Outsider and Bob is a Townsfolk. The Paladin's clues went not-Demon → not-Minion → not-Demon.

On the first night, the Paladin learns Alice and Bob, both Townsfolk. On the second night, the Paladin learns Carol and Dave, both Outsiders. On the third night, the Paladin learns Erin and Frank, both Townsfolk. The Paladin's clues went not-Minion → not-Demon → not-Minion.
paladin.tips:
If you are the Paladin, work out which nights' information means "not Minions" and which means "not the Demon". This is crucial.

If you are the Paladin, one day's information doesn't help you much. Stay alive as long as you can.

If you are the Paladin, your information may seem less useful than learning outright which players are good, or which are Townsfolk. But once you have worked out what your information means, it is a huge help in building the logic of the game.

If you are evil, leaving the Paladin alive is a serious threat to your team. Kill them early.
paladin.bluffing: Your information mostly works like vouching for players. Reporting players who seem good will make you look more like a real Paladin.

alewife.ability: Executed Minions don't die, but are drunk.
alewife.summary: The Alewife saves executed Minions from death, but makes them drunk.
alewife.examples:
The Alewife is in play. On the first day, the Baron is executed but doesn't die; the Baron is now drunk.

The Alewife is in play. On the second day, the Devil's Advocate protects themself and is then executed. They don't die, and the Devil's Advocate is now drunk.
alewife.tips:
If you are the Alewife, remember: as long as you stay sober and healthy, no player who dies by execution is a Minion!

If you are the Alewife and a player doesn't die when executed, be on your guard: they may well be a Minion saved by your ability!

If you are the Alewife: when your ability saves a Minion, that Minion becomes drunk, which means they lose their ability. But if you die, that Minion gets their ability back.

If you are the Alewife, don't reveal your character too early, before any player has survived an execution, because the Demon can attack you to sober up their Minion.

If you are a Minion and you unexpectedly survive your execution, the Alewife is very likely in play. Deny being a Minion and find any other explanation you can for why you didn't die.

If you are a Minion and the Alewife saved you from death, you are drunk from now on. Use your ability carefully so that you don't waste it.
alewife.bluffing:
If you are another character that can make an execution fail to kill, such as the Devil's Advocate, you can claim to be the Alewife: the player who survived their execution is a Minion, which is why you "saved" them.

If you reveal yourself as the Alewife, you are saying that every player who died by execution so far was not a Minion. If people don't accept that, they may not trust you.

warlock.ability: If the Demon kills you, each night from then on, choose a player: they die.
warlock.summary: The Warlock trades their life for forbidden power.
warlock.examples:
On the second night, the Imp kills the Warlock. On the third night, the Warlock is woken and kills the Imp. The game ends and good wins.

On the second night, the Fang Gu kills the Warlock. On the third night, the Warlock is woken and kills the Fortune Teller. On the fourth night, the Warlock is woken and kills the Assassin.

On the second night, the Assassin kills the Warlock. On later nights, the Warlock is never woken.
warlock.tips:
If you are the Warlock, do everything you can to get the Demon to kill you.

If you are the Warlock and the Demon has killed you, you can prove you are the Warlock by killing other players.

If you are the Warlock and the Demon has killed you, you can keep your character hidden and hunt suspected Demons every night. If you kill the Demon, you win outright.

If you are the Warlock, whether you are woken on the night after your death tells you whether your ability triggered.

If you are the Demon, try to avoid killing the Warlock! Triggering their ability has serious consequences: they may kill you on a later night.

If you are the Demon and you killed the Warlock by accident, act as good as you can! If they never attack you, they will actually help you get to the final day faster.
warlock.bluffing: Bluff some other character first, and only admit to being the Warlock after that bluff fails. That looks like something a Warlock would do.

arbiter.ability: Other good players don't die by execution if you nominated them.
arbiter.summary: An execution in the Arbiter's hands never wrongly kills a good player.
arbiter.examples:
On the first day, the Arbiter nominates and executes the Fortune Teller, who doesn't die.

On the second day, the Arbiter nominates and executes the Poisoner, who dies.

On the third day, the Arbiter nominates the Mutant. While defending themself, the Mutant lets slip that they are an Outsider, so the Mutant is executed because of their own ability and dies.
arbiter.tips:
If you are the Arbiter, you can reveal that you are the Arbiter and ask everyone to follow your lead!

If you are the Arbiter, you can hide that you are the Arbiter but do everything you can to get to nominate and execute a player.

If you are the Arbiter and a player you nominated and executed doesn't die, they are most likely good.

If you are the Arbiter and a player you nominated and executed dies, they are very likely evil.

If you are the Demon and an executed player doesn't die, and you can't find another reasonable explanation, the nominator is very likely the Arbiter!

If you are the Demon: leaving the Arbiter to run nominations every day is very dangerous. They will keep protecting good players, and nobody but your teammates will die by execution! Find a way to kill them quickly.
arbiter.bluffing:
If a player you nominate and execute doesn't die, great! It perfectly backs up your Arbiter claim.

If a player you nominate and execute dies, accuse them of being evil!

If you are evil and bluffing the Arbiter, good players may ask you to nominate and execute again and again. If you never manage to protect an executed player, you may lose their trust.

ninja.ability: Each day, if you are the first or the last player to nominate, and the player you nominate is evil, they die tonight.
ninja.summary: The Ninja waits for the chance to assassinate unsuspecting evil players.
ninja.examples:
On the first day, the Ninja is the first to nominate, nominating the Poisoner (evil). That night, the Poisoner dies.

On the first day, the Ninja is the first to nominate, nominating the Saint (good). That night, the Saint doesn't die.

On the second day, the Ninja is the last to nominate, nominating the Imp (evil). That night, the Imp dies.

On the second day, the Ninja is the last to nominate, nominating the Imp (evil). That night, the Imp kills the Ninja first, so the Imp doesn't die.
ninja.tips:
If you are the Ninja, your ability can pick out and kill evil players directly — very powerful! But its conditions are strict: you must make the first or the last nomination, and you must avoid the Demon's suspicion, or they may simply kill you to stop your ability working!

If you are the Ninja, don't startle your prey! Don't act too much like a Ninja, rushing to nominate or organising nominations. The more relaxed you look, the more likely you are to succeed.

If you are the Demon, watch the players who nominate you! If they are the first or last nominator that day and they are the Ninja, you may simply be killed.

If you are the Demon: the Ninja can't use their ability without nominating, so don't worry about players who don't nominate.

If you are the Demon, the best way to deal with the Ninja is to kill them outright: you are faster than they are.

If you are evil, the best way to foil the Ninja is to disrupt their nominations! Nominate first, or deliberately nominate last. But you had better have a good reason, or you may easily be suspected of being an evil player stirring up trouble.
ninja.bluffing:
Deliberately nominate first, or wait until the very end to nominate! It makes you look more like a Ninja.

If you have an ability that causes extra deaths, combining it with a Ninja bluff lets you smear a player you killed as an evil player you assassinated.

vanguard.ability: Each night* before Judgment Day, choose: you can't die tonight, or your 2 alive neighbours can't die tonight.
vanguard.summary: The Vanguard must choose between protecting themself and protecting those beside them.
vanguard.examples:
On the second night, the Vanguard chooses themself, and the Imp attacks the Vanguard that night; the Vanguard doesn't die. On the third night, the Vanguard chooses their neighbours, and the Imp attacks the Fortune Teller sitting next to the Vanguard; the Fortune Teller doesn't die. On the fourth night, the Vanguard chooses their neighbours, and the Imp, sitting next to the Vanguard, kills themself — but the Imp doesn't die.

On every night after Judgment Day arrives, the Vanguard is not woken.
vanguard.tips:
If you choose to protect your neighbours, the nearest alive players on either side of you certainly won't die that night. If they do, consider that you might be poisoned or drunk!

If you think the Demon is more likely to kill you, you can choose to protect yourself!
vanguard.bluffing:
Claim to be the Vanguard, backed by an ability that can cause a night with no deaths!

If you are evil, the Vanguard may be a good choice: you can pretend you guessed wrong, so your ability never triggered.

bellringer.ability: The 1st time you nominate, you may publicly ask the nominee, once, whether they are a particular character: if they lie, you are executed immediately.
bellringer.summary: The Bellringer uses their own body as the hammer, ringing the alarm bell against lies with their life.
bellringer.examples:
On the first day, the Bellringer makes their first nomination, nominating the Fortune Teller, and publicly asks the Fortune Teller player: "Are you the Washerwoman?" The Fortune Teller player answers "No." Nothing happens and the nomination proceeds normally.

On the first day, the Bellringer makes their first nomination, nominating the Baron, and publicly asks the Baron player: "Are you the Washerwoman?" The Baron player answers "Yes." The Bellringer is executed.

On the first day, the Bellringer makes their first nomination, nominating the Drunk, who thinks they are the Washerwoman. The Bellringer publicly asks the Drunk player: "Are you the Washerwoman?" The Drunk player answers "Yes." Nothing happens and the nomination proceeds normally.

On the first day, the Bellringer makes their first nomination, nominating the Baron, and publicly asks the Baron player: "Are you the Washerwoman?" The Baron player refuses to answer. Nothing happens and the nomination proceeds normally.
bellringer.tips:
If you are the Bellringer, it is best to talk things through with the player you are about to nominate first! That avoids them refusing to answer or deliberately answering falsely!

If you are the Bellringer and you weren't executed, the other player may not have lied to you — or your ability is being interfered with.

If you are the Bellringer and you die by execution, the other player certainly lied!

If you are the Bellringer, you can use your ability on the first day to test players who shared information early and verify their characters.

If you are the Bellringer, you can also wait until the middle of the game to use your ability on a more important player. Either way, remember that your ability only works on your first nomination! Don't forget this, or you will waste it.

If you are a good player, you can pretend to be the Bellringer and question a player, to watch how they react.

If you are evil, watch out for the Bellringer: they can easily expose your bluff at the cost of their life, leaving you no defence! If you are cornered, you can refuse to answer. That makes you look more like a guilty evil player, but at least it doesn't let them prove they are the Bellringer. Or you can lie outright! The Bellringer is executed immediately and dies, and either way you certainly won't be executed today!
bellringer.bluffing:
Remember: you don't have the Bellringer's ability, so you can't get yourself executed. But you can act as if the other player didn't lie.

In most cases a good player you question won't lie, but they might lie on purpose to try to trigger your ability. Don't panic: you can calmly drop the Bellringer claim, because anyone can say they are the Bellringer.

faultbot.ability: Each night, you learn if every other Townsfolk player's ability worked normally today.
faultbot.summary: The FaultBot learns whether Townsfolk abilities have gone wrong.
faultbot.examples:
On the first night, the Fortune Teller chooses the good player who registers as the Demon to them, without choosing the Demon, and learns "yes". That night, the FaultBot learns "no".

On the first night, the Empath sits between the Spy and the Saint and learns "0" because of the Spy's ability. That night, the FaultBot learns "no".

On the first night, the Poisoner poisons the Dreamer. The Dreamer chooses the Saint and learns "Saint, Poisoner". That night, the FaultBot learns "yes".

On the second night, the Lycanthrope chooses a good player who registers as evil because of the Lycanthrope's ability; the Lycanthrope doesn't kill that player. That night, the FaultBot learns "no".

On the second night, the Poisoner poisons the Nightwatchman. The Nightwatchman chooses a player, who doesn't learn who the Nightwatchman is. That night, the FaultBot learns "no".

On the first day, the poisoned Savant visits the Storyteller and learns 2 true statements. That night, the FaultBot learns "no".
faultbot.tips:
If you are the FaultBot and you learn "yes", all the Townsfolk are working normally.

If you are the FaultBot and you learn "no", make it public quickly and try to work out with everyone whose ability went wrong.

If you are the FaultBot, note that your own ability can also give false information through poisoning, drunkenness or the Vortox!

If you are the FaultBot, you are a "second-hand information" character: your ability rests on other players' abilities. You are more like an alarm. So you are not that important; what matters are the Townsfolk whose abilities act directly or produce information. Don't be too afraid of dying; you need to give everyone the heads-up quickly.
faultbot.bluffing:
Keep reporting errors! The Townsfolk will be thrown into confusion: whose ability went wrong?

When the Townsfolk's abilities go wrong, claim everything is fine! Cover up the problem!

Don't claim there's no problem when a Townsfolk ability has obviously gone wrong, or you will come under suspicion immediately.

hunter.ability: If a player you nominate dies that night, you are woken to choose a player: they die.
hunter.summary: The Hunter sets a trap and waits for the moment to kill.
hunter.examples:
On the first day, the Hunter nominates the Fortune Teller. That night the Imp kills the Fortune Teller. The Hunter is woken and chooses the Imp; the Imp dies and the game ends.

On the first day, the Hunter nominates the Fortune Teller. That night the Fortune Teller doesn't die, and the Hunter isn't woken.

On the second day, the Hunter nominates the Imp. That night the Imp kills themself. The Hunter is woken and chooses the Fortune Teller, who dies.
hunter.tips:
If you are the Hunter, nominate players you think may die at night! Trigger your ability as often as you can.

If you are the Hunter and you think you are likely to die at night, you can also nominate yourself to try to trigger your ability.

If you are the Hunter and you are woken at night, the player you nominated has died. Choose a player who seems evil if you can!

If you are the Hunter, don't reveal that you are the Hunter. If the Demon knows, they can avoid the players you nominate and never trigger your ability.

If you are the Demon, beware: the Hunter is very dangerous. If they trigger their ability often, they can prove they are the Hunter by killing other players — and they may kill you outright!

If you are the Demon, killing players who weren't nominated that day is a very safe option. So is killing players nominated by someone who doesn't look like the Hunter.

If you are the Demon and you know who the Hunter is, their ability is no longer frightening. You can avoid attacking the players they nominate so it never triggers. Sometimes, though, if you see the Hunter is convinced some good players are evil, you can trigger their ability on purpose and let them help you kill players to speed up the game.
hunter.bluffing:
The Hunter can only kill if the player they nominated dies that night. Keep this firmly in mind.

If the player you nominated died that night but there was no extra death, your Hunter bluff may be in serious trouble.

If you have an ability that causes an extra death at night, the Hunter is a great bluff. Nominate a player, kill them at night, and in the morning claim that the other player who died in the night was your kill.

centaur.ability: Each night, choose a player (not yourself, and not last night's choice): if they are the same character type as the player you chose last night, they die.
centaur.summary: The Centaur kills players who share a character type.
centaur.examples:
On the first night, the Centaur chooses the Fortune Teller. On the second night, the Centaur chooses the Empath, who dies. On the third night, the Centaur chooses the Saint. On the fourth night, the Centaur chooses the Butler, who dies.

On the first night, the Centaur chooses the Scarlet Woman. On the second night, the Centaur chooses the Baron, who dies. On the third night, the Centaur chooses the Imp. On the fourth night, the Centaur chooses the Fortune Teller.

On the fourth night, the Centaur chooses the dead Imp. On the fifth night, the Centaur chooses the alive Imp, who dies. The game ends and good wins.
centaur.tips:
If you are the Centaur and you killed a player, that player is the same character type as the one you chose the night before. Usually both are Townsfolk; occasionally both are Outsiders or Minions.

If you are the Centaur and you chose 2 players who claim to be Townsfolk but both survived, make it public: one of them is not a Townsfolk — most likely an evil player.

If you are the Centaur, choose a player who looks like a Minion! Then choose another player who looks like a Minion the next night! If both really are Minions, you have killed a Minion.

If you are the Demon: the Centaur may keep killing players. If they aren't hitting you or your teammates, leaving them alone may be the better idea.

If you are the Demon and the Centaur chose you or a teammate but nobody died, you can defend yourselves by claiming to be an Outsider or another character of a different type. If necessary, deal with the Centaur at night.
centaur.bluffing:
The Centaur is a very aggressive bluff. Claim to be the Centaur and attack 2 players who claim to be Townsfolk, accusing them of not dying to your ability. It will put a big spotlight on them.

If you can cause an extra death, that is strong evidence to back up a Centaur bluff.

bug_catcher.ability: If you nominate another player, you are woken that night to learn if they are the Demon.
bug_catcher.summary: The Bug Catcher catches the Demon through nominations.
bug_catcher.examples:
On the first day, the Bug Catcher does not nominate. That night, the Bug Catcher is not woken.

On the first day, the Bug Catcher nominates themself. That night, the Bug Catcher is not woken.

On the first day, the Bug Catcher nominates the Baron. That night, the Bug Catcher is woken and learns "no".

On the first day, the Bug Catcher nominates the Fang Gu. That night, the Bug Catcher is woken and learns "yes".
bug_catcher.tips:
If you are the Bug Catcher, nominate a lot! Especially players you suspect of being the Demon! Catch them!

If you are the Bug Catcher, you can also nominate suspicious players only at key moments, which helps you hide that you are the Bug Catcher.

If you are the Bug Catcher and you learn that a player is the Demon, announce it quickly! Rally everyone to deal with them.

If you are a good player, nominate as much as you can to help the Bug Catcher hide!

If you are the Demon and you were nominated by a player who may be the Bug Catcher, you can kill that player at night before you are exposed! Careful! Some "landmines" may pretend to be the Bug Catcher!
bug_catcher.bluffing:
The Bug Catcher usually nominates a lot, so if you bluff the Bug Catcher, remember to nominate often!

If you are the Demon, bluffing the Bug Catcher, then nominating a Minion in the middle or late game and claiming that Minion is the Demon, is a good plan. Whether or not people believe you, at least you look less like the Demon! If they do believe you, they will execute a Minion.

scalebearer.ability: You start knowing a player who is equally far from 2 players of the opposite alignment to them.
scalebearer.summary: The Scalebearer learns a player who is equally far from 2 opponents.
scalebearer.examples:
On the first night, the Scalebearer learns player 3 (good). Players 1 and 5 are both evil, and both are 2 steps from player 3.

On the first night, the Scalebearer learns player 3 (evil). Players 2 and 4 are both good, and both are 1 step from player 3.

On the first night, the Scalebearer learns player 6 (good). Players 1 and 11 are both evil, and both are 5 steps from player 6.
scalebearer.tips: If you are the Scalebearer, the player you learn is either good or evil. If you think they are good, there must be 2 evil players the same distance from them; use elimination to find those 2 evil players. If you can't find 2 evil players at the same distance, the player you learned is evil!
scalebearer.bluffing:
Make up any player: you can then attack pairs of players equally far from them, or attack that player as evil.

If you are the Demon, making up a player who sits midway between 2 Minions may be a good choice.

dame.ability: Each night, you learn an in-play character. When an evil player dies, you become drunk.
dame.summary: Each night the Dame learns an in-play character, but from some point on she is drunk.
dame.examples:
On the first night, the Dame learns the Baron. On the second night, the Dame learns the Chef. On the third night, the Dame learns the Imp. No evil player has died, and the Baron, Chef and Imp are all in play.

On the first night, the Dame learns the Baron. On the second night, the Baron dies and the Dame becomes drunk; the Dame learns the Fortune Teller. On the third night, the Dame learns the Saint. The Baron is in play; the Fortune Teller and the Saint are not.

On the first night, the Dame learns the Fortune Teller. On the second night, the Baron dies and the Dame becomes drunk; the Dame learns the Imp. On the third night, the Dame learns the Saint. The Fortune Teller and the Imp are in play; the Saint is not.
dame.tips:
If you are the Dame: the character you learn on the first night is certainly in play. If it is a good character, the player claiming it should be good.

If you are the Dame, the later the game gets, the less reliable your information is, because over time it becomes more likely that an evil player has died.

If you are the Dame and you know for certain that an evil player has died, your information is worthless from then on.

If you are evil and you know the Dame is in play, dying early may not be a bad idea: it spoils the Dame's information and misleads the good team.

If you are the Demon and you know the Dame is in play, don't fear her. You can attack her, or try attacking one of your own teammates to make the Dame drunk and spoil her information — also a fine choice.
dame.bluffing:
If you are a Minion, the Dame is an excellent bluff. Deliberately reporting characters that seem not to be in play lets you accuse the players who died earlier of including an evil player.

If you are the Demon, the key to bluffing the Dame is reporting fairly believable in-play characters in the early and middle game, then starting to report characters that seem not to be in play in the middle and late game. This helps people trust you more.

notary.ability: Each night*, you learn if the player who died by execution today & their nominator are the same alignment.
notary.summary: The Notary checks whether an executed player and their nominator are on the same team.
notary.examples:
First day: the Baron dies after being nominated by the Fortune Teller. That night, the Notary learns "no".

Second day: the Poisoner dies after being nominated by the Imp. That night, the Notary learns "yes".

Third day: the Chef dies after being nominated by the good Bureaucrat (a Traveller). That night, the Notary is not woken.

Fourth day: the Chef nominates the Imp, who is executed but doesn't die. That night, the Notary is not woken.

Fifth day: nobody nominates. That night, the Notary is not woken.
notary.tips:
If you are the Notary, you only get information when a player dies by execution, so encourage everyone to execute!

If you are the Notary and you learn "yes", the executed player and their nominator are most likely both good, and less likely both evil. If you learn "no", exactly one of them is evil!

If you are a Minion, you can nominate and execute another player, then use the Notary's information to accuse them of being evil! Or you can get them to nominate and execute you, then do the same — this is more believable, since people tend to trust dead players.

If you are a Minion, get the Demon to nominate and execute you. This easily leads the Notary to believe you are both good.

If you are the Demon, nominate carefully! If you nominate and execute a good player, the Notary may well call you out as evil!

If you are the Demon and you know for sure the Notary is in play, nominating and executing an evil player easily builds trust in you.
notary.bluffing:
If you are a Minion, you can be more aggressive when bluffing the Notary! Report lots of "no"s to keep setting players against each other!

If you are the Demon and both the executed player and their nominator look good, reporting "yes" helps you win the other players' trust!

viking.ability: The 1st time you vote while dead, the nominee is executed immediately.
viking.summary: After dying, the Viking can force the execution of another player.
viking.examples:
Second day: the dead Viking uses their vote token to vote for the Imp. It is the Viking's first vote since dying. The Imp has only 1 vote, but is executed immediately and dies.

Fifth day: the dead Viking uses their vote token to vote for the Fortune Teller. It is the Viking's first vote since dying. The Imp had 10 votes earlier and the Fortune Teller has only 4, but the Fortune Teller is executed immediately and dies.
viking.tips:
If you are the Viking, you can only use your ability after you die, so do everything you can to get killed, whether by execution or at night. Dying by execution is usually a poor trade, as it wastes a chance to execute the Demon; if your ability then fails to execute the Demon too, that is 2 executions wasted.

If you are the Viking, you can use your ability in the early or middle game to prove you are the Viking. Or you can use it on the final day to force the execution of a player who didn't get enough votes.

If you are the Demon, it is best to keep the Viking alive: as long as they live, they can't use their ability.

If you are a Minion, you can deliberately provoke the Viking and dare them to execute you. If the Viking asks to be executed that day and uses their ability to execute you the next, the Demon gains at least 2 rounds of executions.
viking.bluffing:
Bluffing the Viking is fairly risky. Vikings generally seek death, and if you stay comfortably alive, it is hard to explain why you are the Viking.

Remember that you don't have the Viking's ability, so even if you die, you can't force an execution. Be prepared for that.

geisha.ability: On your 1st night alive, and on your 1st night dead, you learn an alive player: these 2 players are opposite alignments.
geisha.summary: After dying, the Geisha has learned 2 players of different alignments.
geisha.examples:
On the first night, the Geisha learns player 1 (the Fortune Teller). On the second night, the Geisha dies and learns player 2 (the alive Baron).

On the first night, the Geisha learns player 3 (the Poisoner). On the second day, the Geisha dies by execution, and that night learns player 4 (the alive Saint).

On the first night, the Geisha learns player 1 (the Saint). On the fourth day, the Geisha dies by execution, and that night learns player 2 (the alive Imp).
geisha.tips:
If you are the Geisha and you stay alive all game, you contribute nothing. Find a way to die. But if you think every other player is evil, don't rush to die, or you may lose the game outright.

If you are the Geisha, dying early and dying late mean different things. Early on, you learn 2 players of different alignments, which you can use as fixed points for your reasoning all game. In the middle and late game, the other alive player you learn has a high chance of being the Demon.

If you are the Geisha, you don't always need to rush to die: most players die before the game ends anyway.

If you are the Demon, either deal with the Geisha early or keep them alive until the end. If the Geisha dies in the middle or late game when you are the only evil player left, you are in real danger.
geisha.bluffing:
The Geisha always seeks death. Acting like a player who wants to die makes you look more like the Geisha.

The Geisha works as a backup bluff: if your first bluff falls through, you can explain that you are really the Geisha.

mermaid.ability: Each day, you may publicly accept another player's praise: evil characters' abilities have no effect on them until you accept another player's praise.
mermaid.summary: The Mermaid protects a player who praises her.
mermaid.examples:
On the first day, the Saint publicly praises the Mermaid player: "You look lovely today!" The Mermaid player publicly replies: "Well said — I accept your praise." That night the Imp attacks the Saint, who is protected by the Mermaid and doesn't die.

On the second day, the Fortune Teller publicly praises the Mermaid player: "You understand this game so well — I have a lot to learn from you." The Mermaid player publicly replies: "I love hearing that. I'll protect you, darling." That night the Poisoner chooses the Fortune Teller, but because the Fortune Teller is protected by the Mermaid, they still get true information.

The Fortune Teller is protected by the Mermaid. That night the Poisoner chooses the Fortune Teller, who is not poisoned. Later the Demon attacks the Mermaid, who dies, and the Fortune Teller immediately becomes poisoned again.
mermaid.tips:
If you are the Mermaid, there is little point hiding your character: you need to interact with other players to use your ability, and interacting reveals that you are the Mermaid.

If you are the Mermaid, accept praise from the more important players! Or from whoever gives the praise you like best! Play it however you like, and protect whomever you want!

If you are an important Townsfolk protected by the real Mermaid, your ability certainly can't be affected by the Demon or Minions. Usually you won't die and won't be poisoned, and your information becomes very reliable!

If you are a good player, bluffing the Mermaid now and then helps the real Mermaid hide.

If you are the Demon, several players may claim to be the Mermaid; work out quickly which one is real. Or you could try praising the Mermaid yourself to get her protection, so that no important Townsfolk gets it.
mermaid.bluffing:
Bluff the Mermaid and fool the players you "protect" into thinking their information is highly reliable.

The Mermaid always protects the Townsfolk who seem most important, so pick the more important players. It makes you look more believable.

Players protected by the Mermaid usually don't die at night. Don't attack the players you "protect", or you won't be able to explain it.

psychic.ability: Each night*, choose a player: if they are dead, you learn their alignment.
psychic.summary: The Psychic can check the alignment of dead players.
psychic.examples:
On the first day, the Noble dies by execution. That night, the Psychic chooses the Noble and learns "good".

On the first day, nobody dies. That night, the Psychic chooses the Noble, who is alive, so the Psychic learns nothing.

On the first day, nobody dies. That night, the Psychic chooses the Imp; the Imp chooses themself that night and dies, and the Psychic learns "evil".
psychic.tips:
If you are the Psychic, try to choose dead players who might be evil.

If you are the Psychic: after the first execution you will often have only one confirmed dead player to choose, and sometimes none at all. Then you may need to guess who will die that night and choose them.

If you are the Psychic, the more recent a player's death, the more valuable their alignment is. If you don't want to check a player who died earlier, you can gamble on guessing who will die tonight. But if you guess wrong, you learn nothing.
psychic.bluffing:
The Psychic only learns the alignment of dead players. Be careful not to slip up.

Usually, the Psychic prefers to choose players who died by execution.

marmonk.ability: When the Demon attacks you, an evil player is attacked instead.
marmonk.summary: The MarMonk redirects the Demon's attack.
marmonk.examples:
On the second night, the Imp attacks the MarMonk. The Baron is attacked instead and dies.

On the fourth night, the Fang Gu attacks the MarMonk. The only alive evil player is the Fang Gu, so the Fang Gu is attacked instead and dies. The game ends.
marmonk.tips:
If you are the MarMonk, present yourself as an important character who is afraid of dying, to tempt the Demon into attacking you.

If you are the MarMonk, you can swap claimed characters with some important characters, so that the Demon mistakes you for someone more important and attacks you.

If you are the MarMonk, you can't tell whether your ability triggered. If you find the player who died at night very suspicious, and you were very likely the Demon's target that night, the dead player may be an evil player who died in your place.

If you are the Demon, beware of the MarMonk and avoid attacking them.

If you are the Demon, you can't deal with the MarMonk yourself: have a Minion deal with them, or find a way to execute them.
marmonk.bluffing:
The MarMonk works as a backup bluff, especially after a bluff as an important character fails.

The MarMonk usually doesn't die at night, which you can use to explain why the Demon never seems to attack you.

tanner.ability: You start knowing an evil character that is closest to you.
tanner.summary: The Tanner learns the evil character nearest to them.
tanner.examples:
On the first night, the Tanner learns the Goblin. The Goblin is the evil character nearest the Tanner.

On the first night, the Tanner learns the Fang Gu. The Fang Gu and the Goblin are both 1 step from the Tanner.
tanner.tips:
If you are the Tanner: first, the evil character you learn is certainly in play, which is important information in itself. Second, it is the evil character nearest you, so if you can pin that character on a particular player, every player closer to you than them is good.

If you are the Tanner and you learned a Demon character, the Demon is near you: keep a closer eye on the players around you.

If you are the Tanner and you learned a Minion character, that Minion is closer to you than the Demon is, so the Demon may not be among the players near you.
tanner.bluffing: Bluff the Tanner and report false information, to confuse good's picture of where the evil characters sit.

somnmaid.ability: The 1st time the Demon attacks you, you don't die, and you learn that Demon's character.
somnmaid.summary: The Somnmaid can survive the Demon's attack and learn which Demon it is.
somnmaid.examples:
On the second night, the Imp attacks the Somnmaid. The Somnmaid doesn't die, is woken, and learns the Imp.

On the second night, the Fang Gu attacks the Somnmaid. The Somnmaid doesn't die, is woken, and learns the Fang Gu. On the third night, the Fang Gu attacks the Somnmaid again, and the Somnmaid dies.
somnmaid.tips:
If you are the Somnmaid, bluff an important Townsfolk to tempt the Demon into attacking you.

If you are the Somnmaid and you die at night, either you weren't killed by the Demon's attack or you were poisoned or drunk.

If you are the Somnmaid and you are woken to learn a Demon character, the Demon certainly attacked you last night (or you are poisoned or drunk). Tell everyone what you learned as soon as you can.

If you are the Demon, watch out for the Somnmaid and avoid her if you can. If you attack the Somnmaid, first, you can't kill her; second, you reveal which Demon you are, a huge disadvantage for evil.

If you are the Demon and you have already attacked the Somnmaid once by mistake, and there is no better target, you might as well attack her again to finish her off — especially if everyone believes she is the Somnmaid.
somnmaid.bluffing:
The Somnmaid works as a backup bluff: after a bluff as another character fails, admit that you are really the Somnmaid.

You can reveal that you are the Somnmaid and name the Demon character you "learned". If nobody died last night, this helps you pass as the Somnmaid.

heiress.ability: The 1st time you would die, 2 alive players might die instead.
heiress.summary: Other players might die in the Heiress's place.
heiress.examples:
First day: the Heiress is executed but doesn't die; the Saint and the Noble die instead.

First day: the Heiress is executed and dies.

Second night: the Imp attacks the Heiress, who doesn't die; the Baron and the Fortune Teller die instead.
heiress.tips:
If you are the Heiress and you don't want important Townsfolk to die early, don't reveal your character too soon: the Demon may well kill you, and the Storyteller may have important Townsfolk die in your place.

If you are the Heiress and you want to prove your character, you can try accepting an execution. If the Storyteller has other players die in your place, you are confirmed as the Heiress — though possibly at a heavy price: the deaths of some important characters. Better them than you: for a noble Heiress, what could matter more than clearing your own name? If the lowly ants die, so be it.

If you are the Demon and you know who the Heiress is, attacking her may cause several deaths.

If you are the Demon and you attacked a player who didn't die while 2 other players did, they are most likely the Heiress.
heiress.bluffing:
Publicly claiming to be the Heiress is a deterrent: people may not dare to execute you, especially early in the game.

If several players die, you can come forward as the Heiress and suggest the extra deaths might be your doing. This gives a plausible explanation for last night's extra deaths and keeps good from seeing their real cause.

white_knight.ability: Once per game, a player who is "mad" about wanting to live might not die when executed.
white_knight.summary: The White Knight might save an executed player.
white_knight.examples:
While defending their nomination, the Mastermind is "mad" about wanting to live, and the Storyteller decides to use the White Knight's ability: today the Mastermind is executed but doesn't die.

Today the Tea Lady is "mad" about wanting to live, but the Storyteller decides not to use the White Knight's ability: today the Tea Lady is executed and dies.
white_knight.tips:
If you are the White Knight, persuade players about to be executed to go to their deaths gracefully, if they will listen. This avoids triggering your ability and causing chaos.

If you are the White Knight: once you die, you have no ability. If you want to make sure your ability does nothing, getting yourself killed early is a good way.

If you are the White Knight: a player who survives because of your ability isn't necessarily evil. It may be a good player you all wrongly took for evil. The Storyteller can use this to make you surer that player is evil, so you waste executions on them again and again.

If you are evil, make good use of the White Knight's ability: show a fierce will to live at a key moment, so that the Storyteller helps you survive the execution.

If you are evil, don't pin your hopes on the White Knight on the final day: the Storyteller usually won't let the White Knight's ability work on the last day.
white_knight.bluffing:
If the Devil's Advocate is on your team, the White Knight may be a good bluff: it offers another explanation for why a player protected by the Devil's Advocate didn't die.

If a player survives an execution because of the Devil's Advocate or the Tea Lady — especially one who didn't want to be executed — you can come forward as the White Knight, making it look as if they survived the execution because of your ability.

yeti.ability: Once per game, the Demon may publicly guess that you are the Yeti. If correct, when they are executed that day, you are executed instead. If nobody is executed during the day, your team loses.
yeti.summary: If the Demon finds the Yeti, the Yeti is executed in the Demon's place.
yeti.examples:
Nobody is executed on the first day, so the good team loses.

Today the Demon is about to be executed. The Demon guesses that the Yeti player is the Yeti; when the Demon is executed, the Yeti is executed instead and dies.

Yesterday the Demon died by execution, but the Mastermind was in play, so there is a Mastermind day. Today the Demon is about to be executed. The Demon guesses the Yeti player is the Yeti, the Yeti is executed instead, and evil wins.

Today the Demon is about to be executed. The Demon guesses the Yeti player is the Yeti; then a player makes a new nomination, and today a dead player is executed. The next day the Demon is executed and dies. Good wins.
yeti.tips:
If you are the Yeti and you aren't confident the Demon won't spot you, it is best to get yourself killed early in the game. That avoids a very damaging effect on the final day.

If you are the Yeti, swap claimed characters with a player you trust, to waste the Demon's last guess. Only do this with a good player, of course: if they are evil, you have all but revealed yourself to the Demon.

If you are the Demon, finding the Yeti buys you an extra day of life.

If you are the Demon and the player you believed was the Yeti is already dead, just take a guess when you are about to be executed. You might get lucky.
yeti.bluffing:
The Yeti may not be a great Demon bluff, since usually only evil wants the Yeti alive at the end.

If you are a Minion, revealing yourself as the Yeti in the middle or late game may be a good choice. If the Yeti really is in play, you can force them to reveal themself. If not, you can steer everyone into executing you, helping the Demon survive to the end of the game.

wolfboy.ability: When all other Wolfboys are dead, you become an evil not-in-play Minion. [Several Outsiders might be Wolfboys]
wolfboy.summary: The last surviving Wolfboy becomes an evil Minion.
wolfboy.examples:
A 12-player game: both Outsiders are Wolfboys. On the first day one Wolfboy dies by execution, and the other immediately becomes an evil Poisoner.

A 12-player game with only one Wolfboy in play. The Wolfboy can't become an evil Minion.

A 12-player game with the Baron in play: all 4 Outsiders are Wolfboys. After 3 of them die, the one remaining Wolfboy becomes an evil Scarlet Woman.
wolfboy.tips:
If you are a Wolfboy: there may be several Wolfboys in play, or only you. If all the other Outsiders have died and your character hasn't changed, you are the only Wolfboy, and you can make that public.

If you are a Wolfboy and you die, it is best to reveal your character immediately, because another Wolfboy has very probably become an evil Minion.

If you are a Wolfboy and you become an evil Minion, all the other Wolfboys are dead. From now on, cause as much damage as you can for the evil team.

If you are the Demon, attack the other Wolfboys and keep one alive! They will become a capable teammate.

If you are a Minion, work out quickly who the Wolfboys are and how many there are. If necessary, you can bluff a Wolfboy to draw information out of other players.
wolfboy.bluffing:
Wolfboys usually don't reveal their character early.

Wolfboys usually reveal their character after they die.

The Wolfboy works well as a backup bluff.

If you die, you can claim to be a Wolfboy and attack the other Outsider players.

hells_outcast.ability: Each day, before nominations, a Minion may publicly crown the Hell's Outcast: you immediately turn evil & swap characters with the Demon, who is then drunk.
hells_outcast.summary: If a Minion decides to crown a new king, the Hell's Outcast becomes the new Demon.
hells_outcast.examples:
On the first day before nominations, the Widow publicly announces "I crown the Hell's Outcast". The Hell's Outcast (good) immediately becomes the Vortox (evil), and the Vortox (evil) immediately becomes the Hell's Outcast (evil) and is drunk.

During nominations on the first day, the Widow publicly announces "I crown the Hell's Outcast". Nothing happens.

On the first day before nominations, the Vortox publicly announces "I crown the Hell's Outcast". Nothing happens.

On a day with only 4 players left, before nominations, the Widow publicly announces "I crown the Hell's Outcast". The Hell's Outcast (good) immediately becomes the Vortox (evil), and the Vortox (evil) immediately becomes the Hell's Outcast (evil) and is drunk.

On the second night, the Puck turns the Fortune Teller (good) into the Hell's Outcast (good). In the morning the Puck immediately announces "I crown the Hell's Outcast". The Hell's Outcast (good) immediately becomes the Vortox (evil), and the Vortox (evil) immediately becomes the Hell's Outcast (evil) and is drunk.

A 12-player game. On the first day before nominations, there are 4 evil players: the Widow, 2 Ettins and the Vortox. The Widow (evil) publicly announces "I crown the Hell's Outcast". The Hell's Outcast (good) immediately becomes the Vortox (evil), and the Vortox (evil) immediately becomes the Hell's Outcast (good) and is drunk. (See the jinx with the Ettin in the rules details.)
hells_outcast.tips:
If you don't want to join the evil team as their new leader, you can reveal your character early. With your seat exposed, evil will think carefully before crowning you. Of course, if evil is backed into a corner, they may still risk crowning you, which will most likely drag you down with them. So the safest way is to get yourself killed, which ends any chance of you joining evil.

If you want to join the evil team as their new king, it is best not to reveal your character early. Find a good bluff and wait quietly for a Minion to crown you.

If evil is about to win and the Minions don't seem to plan to crown you, nominate the player you believe is the Demon during the final day's nominations. You have missed the last ride to evil and the Minions have abandoned you: you can only work for good now. Reveal your real character and start attacking the real Demon.

If you are the Demon, none of your Minions is an Ettin, and a Minion has just publicly crowned the Hell's Outcast: if the Hell's Outcast really is alive in play, you are now an evil Outsider. The Minions have a new boss, so drop the Demon mindset and do whatever you still can for evil. If you aren't sure the Hell's Outcast is in play, wait for definite information at night before acting.

If you are the Demon, one of your Minions is an Ettin, and a Minion has just publicly crowned the Hell's Outcast: be very careful. If the Hell's Outcast really is alive in play, you have now become a good, drunk Hell's Outcast!!! (With the Ettin in play, crowning makes the Demon and the Hell's Outcast swap characters and alignments.) If so, evil has thrown you away completely: you are no longer the Demon, nor even evil. If you can be sure this has happened, make it public immediately, and let the Minions who betrayed you and their new king face your revenge.

If you are a Minion, finding out quickly whether the Hell's Outcast is in play, and who it is, is very important. An alive Hell's Outcast is evil's spare tyre and way out. If possible, keep them alive to the end of the game.

If you are a Minion, choosing the right moment to crown the Hell's Outcast is crucial. If the mood of the day is against you and the Demon is very likely to die by execution, crown them publicly before nominations.

If you are a Minion, try to have a dead Minion do the crowning publicly, to keep as much of evil's strength alive as possible.

If you are a Minion, you can publicly crown the Hell's Outcast even when they are not in play, to confuse good about where the Demon is. Or, with the Hell's Outcast in play, have the Demon do the crowning publicly: it doesn't trigger the Hell's Outcast's ability, and good can't tell whether the Demon has moved.
hells_outcast.bluffing:
Revealing yourself as the Hell's Outcast early is risky: people may execute you at once to keep you from joining evil.

Revealing yourself as the Hell's Outcast late in the game may be a good choice, since it can explain some of your odd behaviour early on. As long as nobody publicly crowns the Hell's Outcast this game and the Outsider count isn't abnormal, you will most likely survive to the end.

don_quixote.ability: 1 player registers as a Demon character (the Windmill) to Townsfolk abilities, even if you are dead. You may learn from the Storyteller who the Windmill is; then the Windmill becomes a different player.
don_quixote.summary: Don Quixote chases the wrong target all his life, but never gives up.
don_quixote.examples:
The Sweetheart is Don Quixote's Windmill (registers as a Demon character to Townsfolk abilities). On the first night, the Fortune Teller chooses themself and the Sweetheart and gets the false information "yes".

The Poisoner is Don Quixote's Windmill. On the first night, the Dreamer chooses the Poisoner and gets the false information "Imp, Seamstress".

The Baron is Don Quixote's Windmill. On the first night, the Perfumer chooses the evil character Vortox, and the Baron learns that the Perfumer is in play.

The Noble is Don Quixote's Windmill. On the first night, the Seamstress chooses the Noble and the Dreamer and gets the true information "yes". (Don Quixote's ability only makes the affected player register as a Demon type or Demon character, not as evil.)

The Noble is Don Quixote's Windmill. On the first day, the Bard publicly chooses the Noble; that night the Bard gets the false information "0".

The Noble is Don Quixote's Windmill. On the first day, Don Quixote asks the Storyteller and learns the Noble player; the Windmill immediately moves from the Noble to the Fortune Teller. On the second day, Don Quixote asks the Storyteller and learns the Fortune Teller player; the Windmill immediately moves from the Fortune Teller to the Poisoner.
don_quixote.tips:
As Don Quixote, you may lead good astray in its hunt for the Demon. But never mind! You can visit the Storyteller at any time to learn whom you are affecting, and rule out the false leads. The side effect is obvious, though: a new player becomes your team's interference! Whether to use your ability early to rule out false leads, or use it as little as possible to avoid doing more damage, is up to your wisdom. After all, you are Don Quixote!

The abilities of the Truelove, the Noble, the Seamstress, The Cat Adventurers and the Cowboy are not affected by your ability! They check alignment, or whether someone lied, or whether someone is a Minion — none of which your ability touches!

The player you learn isn't necessarily not the Demon! A cunning Storyteller may deliberately make the Demon your Windmill, to confuse good about which Demon is in play, or to make you think they are just a good player affected by your ability!

If you have pinned down a Demon but have doubts about whether they are affected by your ability, visit the Storyteller! If the Storyteller names a different player, execute them at once!
don_quixote.bluffing:
Bluffing Don Quixote is a great way to excuse a Demon who has been pinned down — whether you are a Minion or the Demon yourself. Once you say you are Don Quixote, logically any player might register as the Demon to Townsfolk abilities. Especially if you pretend to visit the Storyteller and then claim the player you learned is the pinned-down Demon: the Demon's risk of being executed today drops again.

Careful! The player Don Quixote affects doesn't change until they visit the Storyteller, and changes immediately after each visit. Plan what you are going to say, and don't leave obvious holes.

the_cat_chorus.ability: 1 player is drunk. At dusk, the Storyteller might name a song: if the players sing it together successfully, all Townsfolk are unaffected by poisoning & drunkenness until the next dusk.
the_cat_chorus.summary: The Cat Chorus brings powerful music that briefly makes the Townsfolk sober and healthy.
the_cat_chorus.examples:
The Fortune Teller is drunk because of The Cat Chorus. On the first night, the Fortune Teller gets false information. After the first day's execution (at dusk), the Storyteller says: "Night is falling, and tonight we hold a concert! I want to hear 'Blue Lotus'!" Most players join in and it goes well, and the Storyteller announces "The concert was a huge success!" No poisoned or drunk Townsfolk are affected by poison or drunkenness: that night the Monk, poisoned by the Widow, successfully protects a player the Demon attacks, and the Fortune Teller, drunk because of The Cat Chorus, gets true information. At the next dusk, the Monk's poisoning and the Fortune Teller's drunkenness take effect again.

The Cat Chorus is in play. After the second day's execution (at dusk), the Storyteller announces nightfall and picks the song "TNT, We Like You". It goes badly, and the Storyteller announces "The performance failed!" At the dusk after that, the Storyteller picks "Common Jasmine Orange". Most players join in and it goes well, and the Storyteller announces "The concert was a huge success!" No poisoned or drunk Townsfolk are affected by poison or drunkenness.

After the third day's execution (at dusk), the Storyteller announces nightfall and picks "The Maomao Song". Most players join in and it goes well, and the Storyteller announces "The concert was a huge success!" But The Cat Chorus is not actually in play, so poisoned or drunk Townsfolk are still affected.
the_cat_chorus.tips:
If you are The Cat Chorus, remember: one player is drunk because of you.

If you are The Cat Chorus: on a night after a successful sing-along, no Townsfolk is affected by poison or drunkenness (unless you are poisoned or drunk), so that night's information is highly reliable!

If you are The Cat Chorus, party on! Your mission is to lead everyone through one wild night after another! Close your eyes and lead the singing! Don't be shy — nobody can see anybody!

If you are the Demon, kill The Cat Chorus: then even a successful sing-along protects nobody. But because The Cat Chorus dies, the player who was drunk because of them becomes sober.
the_cat_chorus.bluffing:
Lead the party every night: it makes other players more convinced you are The Cat Chorus.

If you bluff The Cat Chorus, you can explain why a Townsfolk's information was "off" on the first night: they could be drunk because of you.

beekeeper.ability: 1 player is poisoned, even if you are dead. Each night, choose a player: if they are poisoned by you, they become healthy.
beekeeper.summary: The Beekeeper poisons a player, but can also cure poisoned players.
beekeeper.examples:
The Noble is poisoned because of the Beekeeper. On the first night, the Noble gets false information. Then the Beekeeper chooses the Noble, who becomes healthy.

The Fortune Teller is poisoned because of the Beekeeper. On the first night, the Fortune Teller gets false information. On the second night, the Fortune Teller gets false information. Then the Beekeeper chooses the Fortune Teller, who becomes healthy. On the third night, the now healthy Fortune Teller gets true information.
beekeeper.tips:
If you are the Beekeeper and you think an important Townsfolk is poisoned because of you, choose them. Whether or not they were poisoned by you before, once you choose them they certainly won't be poisoned by you again.

If you are the Beekeeper, don't choose Townsfolk who have already used their abilities; choose Townsfolk whose abilities are still working.
beekeeper.bluffing: The Beekeeper poisons a player, usually a Townsfolk. If you can't explain a Townsfolk's information, you can claim to be the Beekeeper and say they were poisoned by your ability.

blood_thief.ability: Before Judgment Day, if the only alive evil player dies, you become their character & alignment.
blood_thief.summary: The Blood Thief takes over the game when the whole evil team has fallen.
blood_thief.examples:
On the first day, the Imp dies by execution, but the Imp is not the only alive evil player. The game ends and good wins.

It is Judgment Day, and the Imp is the only alive evil player. That day the Imp dies by execution: the game ends and good wins.

Only 5 players are alive, and the Imp is the only alive evil player among them. That day the Imp dies by execution, and the Blood Thief becomes an evil Imp.

On the third night, 7 players are alive, and the Vortox is the only alive evil player among them. That night the Vortox kills themself, and the Blood Thief becomes an evil Vortox.
blood_thief.tips:
If you are the Blood Thief: usually you only have a chance of turning evil (typically into the Demon) in the middle or late game. If you don't want to become the Demon, find a way to die: then you certainly never will.

If you are the Blood Thief, be careful about revealing your character. If you don't die in the early or middle game, then once the game reaches its later stages you might become the new Demon at any moment. If you have already told other players you are the Blood Thief, you are very easily executed, even if you haven't actually become the Demon.

If you are the Blood Thief and it is the final day and your character still hasn't changed, the Demon is still alive and you have missed the last ride to evil. If you have done anything earlier that muddied the reasoning, reveal your character and explain yourself.

If you are the Blood Thief and you have become evil (usually the Demon), every other evil player is dead and you are the only alive evil player. Fight for yourself.

If you are evil, knowing whether the Blood Thief is in play matters a lot: the Blood Thief gives evil a powerful safety net.

If you are a Minion and you know who the Blood Thief is, do what you can to keep them from revealing their character. You can even "swap characters" with them — each claiming the other's character. You can then come out as the Blood Thief at a convenient moment, laying the groundwork for the Blood Thief later becoming the Demon.

If you are the Demon and you want the Blood Thief to become the new Demon, remember: you must be the last evil player to die. If the other evil players haven't died in time, you can help them along when necessary by killing them at night.

If you are the Demon, getting yourself executed to turn the Blood Thief into the new Demon may be a bit obvious. When necessary, you can kill yourself instead to let the Blood Thief take over — as long as you are already the last alive evil player.
blood_thief.bluffing:
The Blood Thief usually doesn't reveal their character. If you reveal yourself as the Blood Thief early, you are very likely to be executed — which is a fine plan if you are a Minion eager to come out.

Revealing yourself as the Blood Thief in the middle or late game, especially on the final day, leaves good very confused: they can't tell whether you are a Blood Thief who has become the Demon, one who hasn't, or even a Minion posing as the Blood Thief.

two_face.ability: Each night*, you become the opposite alignment to the last player who died by execution.
two_face.summary: Two-Face keeps switching sides between good and evil.
two_face.examples:
On the first day, the Fortune Teller dies by execution. That night, Two-Face turns evil. On the second day, the Poisoner dies by execution. That night, Two-Face turns good. On the third day, the Seamstress dies by execution. That night, Two-Face turns evil.

On the first day, the Fortune Teller dies by execution. That night, Two-Face turns evil. On the second day, the Empath dies by execution. That night, Two-Face's alignment doesn't change. On the third day, the Seamstress dies by execution. That night, Two-Face's alignment doesn't change.
two_face.tips:
If you are Two-Face, you will probably be evil for most of the game, since more good players than evil players usually die by execution.

If you are Two-Face and you are tired of swinging between good and evil, the only sure way to fix your alignment is to die.

If you are Two-Face, you are one of the few Outsiders who can gain a lot of "information" through your ability! If you turn evil at night, the player who died by execution that day was good; otherwise they were evil. But your "information" is hard for others to accept, because Two-Face is extremely hard to trust. And since you may turn evil at any time, think carefully about whether to share what you know to help good.

If you are Two-Face and you are evil on the final day, throw yourself into the vote for evil! If you are good on the final day, you had better be open about it: you could only have turned good because an evil player died by execution the day before. You now need to reason out with everyone who the Demon is and execute them, so that you win with the good team.

If you are good, remember: Two-Face's word can't be trusted. They may betray you at any time.

If you are evil, remember: Two-Face's word can't be trusted. They may betray you at any time.

If you are evil, a reliable way to keep Two-Face on your side is to execute a good player on the second-to-last day. That all but guarantees Two-Face is evil on the final day and votes with evil.
two_face.bluffing:
Two-Face finds it hard to win anyone's trust, and some players always want to execute Two-Face to fix their alignment. So bluffing Two-Face is fairly dangerous.

If you claim to be Two-Face and currently good, you are accusing the last player who died by execution of being evil. If you aren't prepared for that, tread carefully.

mob_lawyer.ability: Each night, you learn a player: tomorrow, if either of you is executed, the other might be executed instead.
mob_lawyer.summary: The Mob Lawyer might interfere with executions.
mob_lawyer.examples:
On the first night, the Mob Lawyer learns player 1 (the Fortune Teller). The next day, player 1 is about to be executed, and the Mob Lawyer is executed instead.

On the first night, the Mob Lawyer learns player 1 (the Fortune Teller). The next day, the Mob Lawyer is about to be executed, and player 1 is executed instead.

On the first night, the Mob Lawyer learns player 1 (the Fortune Teller). The next day, player 1 dies by execution; the Mob Lawyer is not executed in their place.

On the first night, the Mob Lawyer learns player 1 (the Fortune Teller). The next day, the Mob Lawyer dies by execution; player 1 is not executed in their place.
mob_lawyer.tips:
If you are the Mob Lawyer, think each day about whether your "client" is more likely good or evil. If you think your client is evil, don't be afraid to execute them. Even if the Storyteller has you executed instead, you can go after them again the next day. Once you die by execution, the Storyteller can no longer use your ability to protect them! And your death proves you really were the Mob Lawyer.

If you are the Mob Lawyer, be careful about executing yourself. The Storyteller may well "punish" your self-sacrifice by having your client die in your place. That keeps the Mob Lawyer's ability in play for the Storyteller to keep causing chaos with. But it also helps you: it proves you are the Mob Lawyer. If you need to prove yourself, you can try executing yourself — but the Storyteller always has an ulterior motive, and at such moments may choose not to trigger your ability after all.

If you are the Mob Lawyer, reveal your character and the player you learned early, and discuss it with everyone. This stops your ability from disrupting executions, and people may be able to deduce something from the players you learn — though more often than not it leads nowhere.

If you are evil and the Mob Lawyer learned a good player, you can use the excuse that "the Storyteller always shows the Mob Lawyer evil players" to push everyone to execute that good player. If the Storyteller happens to have the Mob Lawyer executed in their place, you can use the same reasoning the next day to demand that player's execution again. This wins evil a big advantage in executions.

If you are evil and you find that the Mob Lawyer learned an evil player, the Storyteller may well trigger the Mob Lawyer's ability to protect that evil player, so that player needn't fear execution as much.

If you are the Demon, try not to attack the Mob Lawyer at night: alive, they cause more chaos. The Storyteller can use their ability to protect evil or to disrupt good's execution plans.
mob_lawyer.bluffing:
Bluff the Mob Lawyer, name your "client" and analyse them. Accuse your "client" of being an evil player the Storyteller wants to protect, and demand their execution.

If you want to bluff the Mob Lawyer, it is best to reveal yourself early and announce your "client" every day. This helps win everyone's trust. But you don't actually have the Mob Lawyer's ability, so your "clients" had better be fringe players; otherwise, when they are executed and you don't die in their place, others will grow suspicious.

pirate_cat_king.ability: Dead players may give up their vote tokens to become Treasure Hunters. When Judgment Day arrives, if you are dead, all Treasure Hunters split 12 vote tokens evenly.
pirate_cat_king.summary: The Pirate Cat King owns all the treasure in the world! Want it? Hand over your vote token!
pirate_cat_king.examples:
On the second day, the dead Poisoner publicly chooses the Pirate Cat King and gives up their vote token. The Storyteller publicly replies, "You are the first Treasure Hunter of this game." That night, the Pirate Cat King dies. On the third day, the dead Fortune Teller publicly chooses the Pirate Cat King and gives up their vote token. The Storyteller publicly replies, "You are the second Treasure Hunter of this game", but since the Pirate Cat King is dead, the Storyteller does not mark the Fortune Teller *TREASURE HUNTER*. When Judgment Day arrives, the Poisoner gets 12 vote tokens and spends them all on a single vote that day.

On the second day, the dead Poisoner publicly chooses the Pirate Cat King and gives up their vote token. On the third day, the dead Fortune Teller does the same. On the fourth day, the dead Saint and Empath do the same. The Storyteller publicly acknowledges each player who gives up a vote token. On a later night, the Pirate Cat King dies. When Judgment Day arrives, the dead Poisoner, Fortune Teller, Saint and Empath get 3 vote tokens each.

On the second day, the dead Poisoner publicly chooses the Pirate Cat King and gives up their vote token. On the third day, the dead Fortune Teller does the same. On the fourth day, the dead Saint and Empath do the same. The Storyteller publicly acknowledges each player who gives up a vote token. When Judgment Day arrives, the Pirate Cat King is still alive, so nobody gets any vote tokens.

On the second day, the dead Poisoner gives up their vote token. On the third day, the dead Fortune Teller gives up theirs. On the fourth day, the dead Saint and Empath give up theirs. The Storyteller publicly acknowledges each player who gives up a vote token, but the Pirate Cat King is not actually in play. When Judgment Day arrives, nobody gets any vote tokens.
pirate_cat_king.tips:
If you are the Pirate Cat King: as a good player, you certainly don't want your "treasure" to end up in evil pockets! So you can stay hidden until you die. Or try to survive until Judgment Day, so that nobody gets your "treasure"! Or privately tell one or two players you think are good to go treasure hunting, so that they claim your "treasure" on Judgment Day!

If you are the Pirate Cat King and, while you are alive, you see a suspected evil player give up their vote token to become a Treasure Hunter, immediately encourage other good players to do the same! If all 12 vote tokens end up with one evil player, you have more or less lost the game!

If you are a good player but not the Pirate Cat King, you can bluff the Pirate Cat King to trick evil players into giving up their vote tokens! But be very careful: good players may be fooled by you too!

If you are evil, keep a close watch on the Outsiders in play and what characters they are. If you find the Pirate Cat King is in play, sending at least one dead player to become a Treasure Hunter is usually a good deal. Even if you get no "treasure" in the end, you have only lost one vote token.
