arthur.ability: Each night*, choose a player: they die. The 1st time Arthur attacks a Minion, Arthur swaps characters with them, and 2 alive players are attacked instead.
arthur.summary: Arthur causes several deaths by "castling" with a Minion.
arthur.examples:
Arthur attacks the Baron. The Baron doesn't die; the Butler and the Poisoner die instead. The former Baron becomes the new Arthur, and the former Arthur becomes the new Baron.

Arthur attacks the Poisoner. The Poisoner doesn't die; Arthur and the Butler die instead. The former Poisoner becomes the new Arthur, and the former Arthur (now dead) becomes the new Poisoner.

The night before, the Baron swapped characters with Arthur and became the new Arthur. That night, Arthur attacks the Poisoner, who dies.
arthur.tips:
If you are Arthur: swapping characters with a Minion is cool! It moves the Demon — but the sudden extra deaths may also reveal that the Demon is Arthur and has moved! So use other characters' extra-death logic as cover for Arthur's castling as best you can!

If you are Arthur, your extra ability isn't just for moving seats! It is also a great way to get extra kills and speed up the game! If only 4 players are alive, castling kills 2 players and can end the game early.

If you are a good player, pay special attention to sudden extra deaths: Arthur may well have castled and slipped away!

If you are a good player, countering Arthur may mean finding every Minion's seat, since you don't know which Minion Arthur will castle with. But if there have been no extra deaths at night, don't worry about the Demon moving: Arthur certainly hasn't castled yet.

corruptus.ability: Each night*, choose a player: they die, no matter what. Dead Outsiders win or lose with you, even if you are dead. [1 or 2 Outsiders in play]
corruptus.summary: The Corruptus bewitches dead Outsiders into serving it.
corruptus.examples:
The Corruptus wins, and all dead Outsiders win too.

The Corruptus loses, and all dead Outsiders lose too.

The Corruptus attacks the Fool, who dies. The Corruptus attacks the Fortune Teller, who is protected by the Tea Lady; the Fortune Teller dies.

The Corruptus attacks the Fortune Teller, who is protected by the Ronin; the Psychopath dies.

Because the Corruptus is in play, there is only 1 Outsider, even though the Baron is in play too.

Because the Corruptus is in play, there are only 2 Outsiders, even though the Baron and the Balloonist are in play too.
corruptus.tips:
If you are the Corruptus, you can kill anyone you like without restraint. But revealing that the Corruptus is in play in the early or middle game may not be wise: good can rule out the other Demons and narrow things down a lot.

If you are the Corruptus, attack Outsiders as much as you can before the game ends! You need some way to tell the Outsiders that the Demon in play is the Corruptus — whether by killing the Fool outright or by having Minions spread the word. This helps evil in the final day's vote.

If you are another evil character and the Corruptus is not in play, you can still fool the Outsiders — especially dead ones — into believing the Demon is the Corruptus. That puts them on evil's side on the final day.

If you are an Outsider, work out carefully which Demon is in play! Whether it is the Corruptus matters a great deal to you. If you are still alive when the game ends, the Corruptus's ability certainly doesn't affect you, so vote for whoever you think is the Demon without worry! If you are dead, be careful: if the Demon is the Corruptus, you must help evil to win in the end.

archlich.ability: Each night*, choose a player: they die. The 1st time each dead player is chosen by the Archlich, that player chooses 2 players: they die.
archlich.summary: The Archlich can pour power into a corpse, giving it deadly strength.
archlich.examples:
On the second night, the Archlich chooses the alive Poisoner, who dies. The next night, the Archlich chooses the dead Poisoner, who chooses the Noble and the Fortune Teller; they die.

On the second night, the Archlich chooses the dead Poisoner, who chooses the Noble and the Fortune Teller; they die. The next day, the Poisoner publicly crowns the Hell's Outcast, who swaps characters with the Archlich and becomes the new Archlich. That night, the new Archlich chooses the dead Poisoner, and nobody dies, because each player can only trigger the Archlich's ability once, whichever Archlich it is.

On the first day, the Noble dies by execution. That night, the Archlich chooses the dead Noble, who chooses the Poisoner and the Archlich. The Poisoner and the Archlich die. The game ends and good wins.

On the first day, the Noble dies by execution. That night, the Archlich chooses the dead Noble, who chooses 2 dead players, so nobody dies. The next night, the Archlich chooses the dead Noble again, and the Noble is not woken, because each player can only trigger the Archlich's ability once.
archlich.tips:
As the Archlich, you must learn to use corpses. If you only choose alive players and never dead ones, you are just an ordinary Demon with no special power. Every dead player is material for you: think about how to use the corpses to paint a beautiful canvas of slaughter.

Choosing a dead evil player is a smart move: they will kill with your interests in mind and won't reveal you. But there are only ever a few dead evil players.

There is no shortage of dead good players; you can hardly choose them all. But choosing a dead good player may come at a price. First, good learns you exist: a good player you chose will almost certainly announce that the Archlich chose them. Second, they may choose players you'd rather they didn't — evil players, or dead players. They may even kill you outright. So unless you have a particularly evil, well-rounded plan, be careful about choosing dead good players.

If you suspect several deaths were caused by the Archlich and no player claims to have been touched by the Archlich, the earlier dead players certainly include an evil player — most likely one who died by execution!

Don't firmly believe a dead player who claims the Archlich chose them. Evil players can use this deliberately to mislead good about which Demon is in play, or to lure you into executing a good player.

If you are a dead good player woken that night by the Archlich's ability, make your choice carefully. Choose 2 dead players to avoid needless deaths, or choose the players you believe are evil to cut down their numbers as far as possible? It is entirely up to you.

If you are a dead good player chosen by the Archlich, choose the players you think might be the Archlich! Let the reckless Demon reap what it sows!

hydra.ability: Each night*, choose a player: they die. If you die by execution before Judgment Day, a good player & an evil player become Hydras.
hydra.summary: Execution makes the Hydra "split and multiply".
hydra.examples:
On the first day of the game, the Hydra dies by execution. The Fortune Teller becomes a Hydra (good) and the Baron becomes a Hydra (evil). That night, each of them kills a player.

With 5 players left alive, the Hydra dies by execution. The dead Noble becomes a Hydra (a dead, good Hydra) and the alive Baron becomes a Hydra (an alive, evil Hydra).

On Judgment Day, the Hydra dies by execution. The game ends and good wins.
hydra.tips:
If you are the Hydra, as a Demon with unmatched staying power, you don't fear death much. You can boldly attack other players or do other high-risk things. So what if you are executed? As long as evil still has someone alive, the game doesn't end.

If you are an alive evil player and you are told you have become a Hydra, a good player has certainly become a Hydra too — whether they are dead or alive now, you can't know. A dead Hydra usually poses little threat; they will just tell everyone their character changed. But an alive good Hydra is a big wild card: they may kill other good players, or your teammates, or even you. Whether to let them kill freely and help you end the game sooner, or to kill them quickly and remove the wild card, is up to you depending on the game.

If you are a dead evil player, claiming at the right moment that you have become a Hydra is an interesting tactic. Good players can't tell whether you are telling the truth. If they believe you, they accept that yesterday's executee was the Hydra, which leads them into wrong conclusions and even defeat.

If you are an alive evil player, you can also claim at the right moment that you have been turned into a Hydra. That means explaining whom you chose last night as a Hydra, so prepare your story. Good may ask you to kill yourself at night; if you never die, good will find it hard to keep trusting you.

If you are an alive good player and you are told you have become a Hydra, that is interesting. You can kill yourself that night and tell everyone as soon as it is day. That avoids adding to the chaos and lets everyone know yesterday's executee was the Hydra. Or you can quietly say nothing and kill whomever you like at night. Just remember to kill yourself before the final day, or good can't win while you exist. Please don't try to get yourself executed: that creates more Hydras.

If you are a dead good player and you are told you have become a Hydra, you had better tell everyone about the change as soon as it is day: the Demon having moved is important information. Also, the Storyteller choosing a dead good player to become a Hydra may mean the game is nearly over and good's time is running out.

If an alive player claims to be good and to have become a Hydra, executing them may not be a good idea, because executing a Hydra on any day but the final one triggers the split, even if it is a good Hydra. It is better to have them kill themself at night before evil can win, since good can't win while any Demon is alive.

In the vast majority of cases, good only wins immediately if the Hydra is executed on the final day. But that doesn't make executing the Hydra early a bad idea: good may get an alive good Demon out of it! That is a big temptation — good can then kill anyone it wants. So if you find the Hydra early, executing it at once or saving it for the final day are both workable choices.

chimera.ability: Each night*, choose a Demon character other than the Chimera (not either of your previous 2 choices): you have that character's ability until dusk. [-1 Outsider]
chimera.summary: The mighty hybrid Chimera can use the abilities of every other Demon on the script.
chimera.examples:
On the 2nd night, the Chimera chooses the Vortox, and every Townsfolk's information that night is wrong. On the 3rd night, the Chimera chooses the Archlich; that night it chooses a dead Minion, who chooses 2 other players and kills them. On the 4th night, the Chimera chooses the Hydra; it is executed the next day, and a good player and an evil player become Hydras.

On the 2nd night, the Chimera chooses the Vortox. On the 3rd night, the Chimera wants the Vortox again, but its choice must differ from both previous choices, so it chooses the Archlich. On the 4th night, the Chimera wants the Archlich, but its choice must differ from both previous choices, so it can only choose the Hydra. On the 5th night, the Chimera can only choose the Vortox. On the 6th night, the Chimera can only choose the Archlich.

Because the Chimera is in play, there is 1 fewer Outsider than the default.
chimera.tips:
The Chimera is very powerful: it can use the abilities of every other Demon on the script. But it can only hold one ability a day, and once the Chimera's cycle of abilities is set, it can't change. Think hard about how to choose and use your abilities.

If you sense you will be executed tomorrow, taking the Hydra's ability that night is a very good move. It helps keep the Demon going.

Because of you, there is 1 fewer Outsider than the default, so whether to have a teammate claim to be an Outsider matters a lot.

If you are a good player and the Demon is the Chimera, then on one of the second to fourth nights the Chimera chose the Vortox, meaning every Townsfolk's information that night is certainly wrong. If on some night the Townsfolk's information suddenly all goes wrong, consider that the Demon may be the Chimera.

Once the Chimera's cycle forms, it is fixed. If you can be sure the Chimera took the Vortox's ability on the second night, the Chimera can only take the Vortox's ability on the fifth and eighth nights too. (Unless the Hell's Outcast moved the Demon: a Chimera newly entering play resets the cycle.)

If you are a good player and the number of Outsiders is below the default, the Demon in play is very likely the Chimera.

If both the Chimera and the Cyclops are in play, the Outsider count doesn't go down. Don't conclude the Demon isn't the Chimera just because the Outsider count is right.

skeleton_king.ability: Each night*, choose a player: they die. When you win by the usual conditions, Townsfolk who gave up their vote tokens also win. [+1 Outsider]
skeleton_king.summary: The Skeleton King leads the Townsfolk who surrender to victory alongside him.
skeleton_king.examples:
Because the Demon is the Skeleton King, there are 3 Outsiders — 1 more than the default 2.

On the fifth day, the dead Dreamer and Washerwoman, who still hold their vote tokens, publicly surrender to the Skeleton King and give up their vote tokens. That day the Fortune Teller is executed, leaving only the Skeleton King and the Seamstress alive: evil wins, and so do the Dreamer and the Washerwoman.

On the final day, every dead Townsfolk publicly surrenders to the Skeleton King and gives up their vote token. Evil wins, and because of the Skeleton King's ability, the dead Townsfolk who gave up their vote tokens win too.
skeleton_king.tips:
With the Skeleton King in play, a Townsfolk who gives up their vote token is guaranteed to win — a huge temptation for Townsfolk players. So whether or not the Demon in play is the Skeleton King, convincing dead Townsfolk that it is, so that they surrender, gains evil a huge advantage: Townsfolk who gave up their vote tokens certainly won't take part in the final day's vote.

The Skeleton King adds an Outsider, so you or a teammate bluffing an Outsider is a good way to fake the Skeleton King being in play.

If you are the Skeleton King, you can have a Minion loudly announce that the Demon in play is the Skeleton King. It splits the good team with ease.

If you are the Skeleton King, having most of the Outsiders survive into the late game is very good for you. Dead Townsfolk are always wavering; if only Outsiders survive, they are the only ones left to unite against you.

If you are a Townsfolk, you believe the Demon in play is the Skeleton King, and you make it to the final day, persuading the other dead players to vote is the most important thing.

Outsiders aren't affected by the Skeleton King's ability and are a key force against it. Winning the Outsiders' support greatly helps you gain the upper hand against the Skeleton King.

Dead Townsfolk can't be trusted: even if the Demon isn't the Skeleton King, they may be fooled into sitting out the final day's vote.

In a 12-player game with the Skeleton King in play, there is usually 1 Demon, 2 Minions and 3 Outsiders. Even if every Townsfolk has died, good only needs one dead Townsfolk's vote to execute the Skeleton King on the final day. So don't fear the Skeleton King too much: persuading the wavering dead Townsfolk is the key.

the_sea_born.ability: Each night*, choose a player: they die. The Storyteller decides which Minion abilities they have, and helps you win as best they can. [No Minions in play. Any number of Outsiders]
the_sea_born.summary: The Sea-born has no Minions; the Storyteller helps them with Minion abilities.
the_sea_born.examples:
On the first night, the Storyteller wakes the Sea-born, who learns 3 bluffs. The Storyteller uses the Poisoner's ability to choose the Fortune Teller, who gets false information. On the second night, the Sea-born points to the Noble; the Storyteller shakes their head and points to the Fortune Teller, and the Sea-born takes the advice and chooses the Fortune Teller, who dies. On the third day, the Sea-born quietly visits the Storyteller in private and gets some advice.

On the first night, the Storyteller uses the Poisoner's and the Cerenovus's abilities to choose a player each. On the second night, the Storyteller uses the Poisoner's, the Cerenovus's and the Assassin's abilities to choose a player each.

On the first day, the Sea-born quietly visits the Storyteller in private, and the Storyteller gives them some advice on bluffing and playing.

With the Sea-born in play, the starting number of Outsiders is 1 more than the default.
the_sea_born.tips:
If you are the Sea-born, the Storyteller is your only teammate and will help you as much as they can. When you get the chance, try to talk with them at night or during the day and listen to their advice. It will help you win.

If you are a good player, remember: the Sea-born has no Minions. If you can't seem to find any evil players, consider the Sea-born.

If you are a good player and important Townsfolk keep dying early, or more Minion abilities are being used than there should be Minions, be wary that the Demon may be the Sea-born.

If the Demon is the Sea-born, nearly every player in play is good, and an evil Storyteller is wielding Minion abilities to deceive you. You will have enough time to find the one evil player.

dretch.ability: Each night*, a player dies. After being nominated, you may call for help: if fewer alive players are evil than good, a Minion becomes a Dretch.
dretch.summary: Push a Dretch too hard and it calls in more Dretches!
dretch.examples:
On the first day, the Dretch is nominated and says: "Coo coo coo, quack quack quack! Help me, help me!" The Storyteller responds: "I hear someone calling their Dretch companions!" Among alive players there are 9 good and 3 evil; evil is fewer, so the Baron becomes a Dretch.

On the third day, the Dretch is nominated and says: "K'zhak! K'zhak! Dretch! Dretch!" The Storyteller responds: "They are calling their companions like a Dretch!!" Among alive players there are 5 good and 3 evil; evil is fewer, so the Baron becomes a Dretch. That day the Butler dies by execution. That night the Dretches kill a good player and an evil player.

On the fifth day, the Dretch is nominated and says: "I call my companions!" The Storyteller responds: "Noted — you have called your companions." Among alive players there are 2 good and 2 evil; since evil is not fewer than good, nobody becomes a Dretch. That day the Dretch dies by execution; the game ends and good wins.
dretch.tips:
If you are the Dretch and you think you will be executed today, call your companions! It amounts to a confession — admitting you are evil — but it beats losing outright.

If you are the Dretch, keep an eye on the balance of the remaining players. If evil is not fewer than good, you can't call in more companions!

If you are the Dretch, calling your companions with 3–4 players left alive is pointless: with 2 evil players alive, good can't still outnumber evil. And if you are the only evil player, there is no alive Minion to take your place. Of course, if your aim is to bluff — to play a Minion drawing attention and hoping to be executed in the Demon's place — it may still work.

If you are the Dretch and you are sure you won't be executed today, nominating yourself and calling your companions is a bold, aggressive plan. Several alive Demons give evil a big advantage: several players die each night, bringing the final day much sooner.

If you are a Minion and the Demon has already called their companions today, consider calling yours straight away! If you are the newly summoned Dretch, your call creates yet another Dretch! Several alive Dretches give evil a big advantage. But careful: the Storyteller may use the Dretches' ability to kill some evil players at night.

If you are a Minion and your Demon boss is in danger, you can deliberately call your companions to force the others to execute you! Your Demon boss is then safe for now — at least for today.

tzeentch.ability: Each night*, choose a player: they die. When you learn the Demon info, you get extra bluffs; choose 1 of them: you gain that character's ability.
tzeentch.summary: The Tzeentch has the perfect bluff.
tzeentch.examples:
On the first night, the Tzeentch learns 4 bluffs: the Gossip, the Dreamer, the Innkeeper and the Saint. The Tzeentch chooses the Dreamer and gains its ability. That night the Tzeentch is woken for the Dreamer's ability, chooses the Fortune Teller player, and learns "Fortune Teller, Baron".

On the first night, the Tzeentch learns 6 bluffs: the Gossip, the Dreamer, the Innkeeper, the Saint, the Golem and the Washerwoman. The Tzeentch chooses the Gossip and gains its ability. On the first day, the Tzeentch makes a true public statement (the Gossip's ability). That night the Tzeentch is woken and attacks a player; then another player dies because of the Gossip's ability.

On the first night, the Tzeentch learns 5 bluffs: the Gossip, the Dreamer, the Golem, the King and the Choirboy. The Tzeentch chooses the Golem and gains its ability. On the first day, the Tzeentch nominates the Baron player, and the Baron dies. Because of the Golem's restriction, the Tzeentch can't nominate again for the rest of the game.
tzeentch.tips:
If you are the Tzeentch, you get extra bluffs! That gives you more room to manoeuvre. Don't be stingy — share those bluffs with your Minions.

If you are the Tzeentch, you can perfectly pass as one of your bluff characters — a great advantage. You can learn other players' characters just like a real Dreamer, or cause extra deaths just like a real Gossip. Prefer bluff characters that let you "prove" yourself! Once you have "proved" yourself, people will believe you more easily!

If you are the Tzeentch, you don't have to claim the bluff you chose. You can use its ability to cause trouble on the quiet — for example, using the Innkeeper's ability to make someone drunk, or the Gossip's ability to cause extra deaths!

If you are a good player, treat players who have "proved" themselves with care. They aren't necessarily the character they "proved" — they may be the Tzeentch! For example, a Virgin or Golem whose ability fired, or a Nightwatchman who has already used their ability.

If you are a good player and you want to argue that the Demon in play is the Tzeentch, then no other Demon's ability can be working, since other Demons can't be in play alongside the Tzeentch! So if you think a player who has proved themself is the Tzeentch, first consider whether that holds up with no other Demon ability in play.

tornado.ability: Each night*, choose a player: they die. Each dusk*, you swap characters with the nearest alive evil player clockwise from you.
tornado.summary: The Tornado keeps changing seats, always in the same direction.
tornado.examples: On the first day, a player dies by execution. At nightfall, the Tornado player (player 1) swaps characters with the Poisoner player (player 3). The Tornado player (player 1) is woken and learns they are now the Poisoner; the Poisoner player (player 3) is woken and learns they are now the Tornado. That night the new Poisoner (player 1) poisons a player, and the new Tornado (player 3) kills a player. After the next day's execution, the Tornado player (player 3) swaps characters with the Baron player (player 4); night actions omitted. After the following day's execution, the Tornado player (player 4) swaps characters with the Poisoner player (player 1).
tornado.tips:
If you are the Tornado: the Tornado moves every day, so agree on a plan with your teammates to avoid the Demon dying suddenly.

If you are the Tornado, you can be more aggressive in the first few days: you will soon stop being the Demon, so you can play yourself as a Minion.

If you are a Minion and the Demon is the Tornado, you will soon become the new Tornado. Careful! Don't talk yourself out of the game!

If you are a good player: the Tornado moves every day, so the usual methods may struggle to pin down the Demon. You must predict where the Demon will move and deal with the likely evil players in advance!

echo.ability: Each night*, choose a character: they die. If that character is not in play, choose 1 extra character the next night (this stacks).
echo.summary: The Echo builds up extra attacks, and attacks particular characters directly.
echo.examples:
On the second night, the Echo chooses the Fortune Teller, who is in play and dies. On the third night, the Echo chooses the Saint, who is in play and dies.

On the second night, the Echo chooses the Fortune Teller, who is not in play, so nobody dies. On the third night, the Echo chooses the Saint and the Fortune Teller; neither is in play, so nobody dies. On the fourth night, the Echo chooses the Baron, the Empath and the Washerwoman. All three are in play, and those players die.
echo.tips:
If you are the Echo, send off the characters you find most troublesome — don't hesitate!

If you are the Echo and you aren't sure whether a player is really the character they claim, choose that character at night to test it. If they die, they were that character. If they weren't, no matter: you don't waste your attack.

If you are the Echo, watch for players who died "unexpectedly". They may have swapped claims with someone, and they are the one you were really after.

If you are the Echo, don't keep choosing the same not-in-play character, unless you want to build up power!

If you are the Echo and the script has a Demon that can attack several players in one night, you can deliberately choose a not-in-play character (one of your bluffs, say), so that nobody dies! But the night after, you can attack several players!

If you are a good player and important Townsfolk died in the first few nights, consider that the Demon may be the Echo!

If you are a good player and a night passes with no deaths, the Echo may be building up power! Beware of them ending the game early!

kraken.ability: Each night*, choose a player: they die. If you would die before Judgment Day, you feign death instead. While feigning death, you can only kill your alive neighbours.
kraken.summary: The Kraken can feign death and lie in wait among the crowd.
kraken.examples:
On the first day, the Kraken is executed. They are still alive, but to the other players they are dead (feigning death). That night they kill the Fortune Teller sitting next to them. On the second day, the Kraken, still feigning death, is executed again. The Kraken truly dies, and good wins.

On the second night, the Kraken kills themself (and begins feigning death). In the morning the Storyteller announces their death. On every night after that, the Kraken kills one of their alive neighbours.

On the fourth night, the Kraken, feigning death, chooses an alive player who is not their neighbour. That player doesn't die.

The Storyteller announces that Judgment Day has arrived. That day the Kraken is executed and dies, and good wins.
kraken.tips:
If there aren't enough dead players around you, don't kill yourself lightly. While feigning death you can only kill your alive neighbours, and if everyone dying at night sits next to you, it points very clearly to you being a Kraken feigning death.

Even without feigning death early, you are very strong. You don't have to feign death at all; keep it as your last resort.

If you are a good player and the players who die at night always cluster around one particular dead player, don't hesitate: point out that they may be a Kraken feigning death and try to execute them again.

If you are a good player: the Kraken is very hard to kill, but once feigning death, it can only kill its alive neighbours. So if, after the death of a player you suspect is the Kraken, a player who is not their neighbour dies that night, they certainly aren't the Kraken.

minotaur.ability: Each night*, choose an alive player: they die. Before Judgment Day, if every evil player has died by execution, your team wins.
minotaur.summary: The Minotaur feigns defeat, luring good into a trap that ends in its loss.
minotaur.examples:
A 12-player game. On the first day, the Baron dies by execution. On the second day, the Poisoner dies by execution. On the third day, the Minotaur dies by execution, and evil wins.

A 15-player game. On the first day, the Baron dies by execution. On the second day, the Fortune Teller dies by execution. On the third day, the Poisoner dies by execution. On the fourth day, the Spy dies by execution. On the fifth day, the Minotaur dies by execution, and evil wins.

A 10-player game. On the first day, the Baron dies by execution. On the second day, the Fortune Teller dies by execution. On the third day, the Poisoner dies by execution. On the fourth day — Judgment Day — the Minotaur dies by execution, and good wins.
minotaur.tips:
If you are the Minotaur, decide at the start of the game how you mean to win. If you want the special win, every Minion must go bravely to their death, and you need to tell all of them so.

If you are the Minotaur and your special-win plan is interrupted — say a Minion dies other than by execution, or there aren't enough executions left before Judgment Day to execute the remaining evil players — change strategy at once and survive to the end the traditional way.

If you are another Demon, you can still have your Minions go to their deaths at key moments even though you aren't the Minotaur. Good will think the Demon in play is the Minotaur and change their execution strategy, which buys you more room to survive.

If you are a good player and you think good is steamrolling ahead, executing one suspected evil player after another, watch out! The Demon in play is very likely the Minotaur. If the Minotaur is in play and is executed as the last evil player, you lose. If you suspect the Demon may be the Minotaur, change your execution strategy: execute the most Demon-like player earlier, or save the suspected Demon for execution on Judgment Day.

nurgle.ability: Each night*, choose a player: they die, and their neighbours are poisoned until your next attack.
nurgle.summary: The Nurgle's attacks kill, and also poison the players around the victim.
nurgle.examples:
On the second night, the Nurgle attacks the Saint, who dies. The Fortune Teller sits on the Saint's left and the Baron on their right; the Fortune Teller and the Baron are poisoned.

On the second night, the Nurgle attacks the Fortune Teller. The Nurgle sits on the Fortune Teller's left and the Klutz on their right; the Nurgle and the Klutz are poisoned. On the fourth night, the Nurgle attacks the Noble — by now the Nurgle and the Klutz are healthy again — and the Noble dies. The players on both sides of the Noble are poisoned, even though both are dead.

On the third night, the Nurgle attacks the already dead Fortune Teller. The Empath sits on the Fortune Teller's left and the Klutz on their right; the Empath and the Klutz are poisoned.

On the third night, the Nurgle attacks the Klutz, who is protected by the Monk and doesn't die. The Empath sits on the Klutz's left and the Fortune Teller on their right; the Empath and the Fortune Teller are poisoned.
nurgle.tips:
If you are the Nurgle, plan your attacks so that your deaths and your poison both work as efficiently as possible.

If you are the Nurgle: your attacks may poison players who aren't Townsfolk, which may not be good for you. Try not to interfere with abilities that matter to you.

If you are the Nurgle, attacking dead or protected players now and then, to poison at just the right moment and disrupt the game, is also a good choice.

If you are a good player: the Nurgle's poison always lingers around players who die at night. So if both players next to you are still alive, you needn't worry about being poisoned by the Nurgle.

If you are a good player: the Nurgle usually avoids attacking the players next to an important Minion, so as not to interfere with its ability. If you can be sure the Demon in play is the Nurgle, a player claiming to be an important Townsfolk who stays alive, with both neighbours alive too, is very suspicious.

khorne.ability: Each night*, choose 2 players: they die. If a good player died today, 1 of the players you choose tonight doesn't die.
khorne.summary: The Khorne both kills and protects players.
khorne.examples:
On the first day, a good player dies by execution. That night the Khorne chooses the Fortune Teller and the Noble; the Noble dies and the Fortune Teller doesn't.

On the first day, a good player dies by execution. That night the Gambler guesses a character wrongly, and the Khorne chooses the Fortune Teller and the Gambler. The Fortune Teller dies and the Gambler doesn't (because of the Khorne's ability; see the rules details).

On the first day, an Outsider dies by execution. That night the Khorne chooses the Fortune Teller and the Noble, and the Fortune Teller dies. Then the Godfather chooses the Noble, and the Noble doesn't die.

On the first day, the Golem nominates and kills a good player. That night the Khorne chooses the Fortune Teller and the Noble; the Fortune Teller dies and the Noble doesn't.

On the second day, only a good player is executed, and they don't die. That night the Khorne attacks 2 players, and both die.

On the third day, only an evil player dies by execution. That night the Khorne attacks 2 players, and both die.

On the fourth day, nobody is executed. That night the Khorne attacks 2 players, and both die.
khorne.tips:
If you are the Khorne, your protection can keep players who should die at night alive, sowing some confusion — for example, protecting a Gambler who guessed wrongly, or a Minion targeted by a Townsfolk hunting evil.

If you are the Khorne: if a good player died during the day, you can't kill one particular player with certainty that night. So choose 2 players of equal importance, to make sure your kill is worth it.

If you are the Khorne and an evil player died by execution that day, you can hide your strength: deliberately choose a dead or protected player so that only one player dies. That lets you pose as another Demon, or lead people to believe the executed player was good.

If you are the Khorne, don't fear good not executing anyone, or executing someone who doesn't die: it lets you kill several players that night. But it may also reveal that the Demon is the Khorne.

If you are a good player and several players often die at night for no apparent reason, consider that the Demon may be the Khorne.

If you are a good player and you think the Demon in play is the Khorne, but only one player died at night, the player executed that day may have been good. If 2 or more players died at night, the player executed that day was very likely evil.

If you are a good player and you think the Demon in play is the Khorne, try to execute someone every day. Even if you don't choose a player to execute, the Khorne will kill several players at night. Better for the group to decide together than to let the Khorne choose.

slaanesh.ability: Each night*, choose a player: they die, and you may have them learn that you are Slaanesh. The last player to learn you are Slaanesh wins or loses with you, even if you are dead.
slaanesh.summary: Slaanesh can charm the players it kills.
slaanesh.examples:
Second night: Slaanesh kills and charms the Fortune Teller, who learns who Slaanesh is. Slaanesh charms nobody else after that. The game ends and evil wins; the Fortune Teller wins too.

Second night: Slaanesh kills and charms the Fortune Teller, who learns who Slaanesh is. Slaanesh charms nobody else after that. The game ends and good wins; the Fortune Teller loses.

Second night: Slaanesh kills and charms the Fortune Teller, who learns who Slaanesh is. Third night: Slaanesh kills and charms the Saint, who learns who Slaanesh is. Fourth night: Slaanesh kills and charms the Exorcist, who learns who Slaanesh is. Slaanesh charms nobody else after that. The game ends and evil wins; the Exorcist wins too.
slaanesh.tips:
If you are Slaanesh, you can charm the players you kill from the start of the game, which quickly wins you more "help". But as the game goes on, earlier charmed players may sense that "something is off" as the game tilts one way, and easily realise you have betrayed them. If they become sure you have charmed someone else, they may come forward and name you as Slaanesh — very bad for you.

If you are Slaanesh, you can charm the players you kill in the middle or late game instead. They will serve you more loyally, since you are less likely to charm anyone else afterwards.

If you are Slaanesh, you can charm just one player or several. The more you charm, the bigger the gains — and the bigger the risk!

If you are a good player, remember: good players who didn't die at night certainly can't have been charmed by Slaanesh. They can be trusted.

If you are a good player, watch how the players who died at night behave to judge whether they have been charmed! If several dead players act strangely, hesitate, or keep changing sides, they have very likely been charmed by Slaanesh!

If you are a good player and you have learned who Slaanesh is, Slaanesh has charmed you! Don't name Slaanesh straight away: until Slaanesh charms someone new, your fates are tied together. If you find a new player has been charmed, don't hesitate — name Slaanesh at once and try to execute them.

tango.ability: During setup, the Storyteller publicly names a character: if it is in play, there is 1 more or 1 fewer Outsider.
tango.summary: The Tango makes certain characters add or remove an Outsider.
tango.examples:
Before the game, the Storyteller publicly names the Poisoner as the "lead dancer". The Poisoner is in play this game, so there is 1 more Outsider than usual.

Before the game, the Storyteller publicly names the Imp as the "lead dancer". The Imp is in play this game, so there is 1 fewer Outsider than usual.

Before the game, the Storyteller publicly names the Fortune Teller as the "lead dancer". The Fortune Teller is not in play this game, so the number of Outsiders doesn't change.

ward_surveillance.ability: The Storyteller might tell the Demon or Minion players anything about the Lunatic. The Lunatic might learn that other players are the Lunatic.
ward_surveillance.summary: The Ward Surveillance makes it hard for the Lunatic to escape.
ward_surveillance.examples:
Alice is the Demon and Bob is the Lunatic. On the first night, Alice learns that Bob is the Lunatic, that the Minion Bob learned is Alice herself, that Bob's bluffs are the Ravenkeeper, the Monk and the Magician, and that Bob learned player 1 is the Lunatic.

Alice is the Lunatic and Bob is the Exorcist. On the first night, Alice learns that Bob is the Lunatic, that the Minion Bob learned is Alice herself, that Bob's bluffs are the Ravenkeeper, the Monk and the Magician, and that Bob learned player 1 is the Lunatic. Some of what Alice learns is true and some false, because Alice is the Lunatic.

Alice is the Pukka and Bob is the Lunatic. On the first night, Alice learns that Bob is the Lunatic, and that Bob thinks he is the Pukka and chose player 1.

Alice is the Demon and Bob is the Lunatic. On the first night, Alice learns that Bob is the Lunatic and nothing else about the Lunatic, because the Storyteller chose not to share more.

Alice is the Mastermind and Bob is the Lunatic. On the first night, Alice learns that Bob is the Lunatic, that the Minions Bob learned are Alice herself and player 1 (the Storyteller is fooling the Lunatic into thinking the Magician is in play), and that Bob's bluffs are the Ravenkeeper, the Monk and the Bard.

lethe.ability: Possibly: the Demon & Minions think they are good characters, and the Storyteller uses their abilities for them. The game ends only when all evil players are dead, and then all players win.
lethe.summary: The Demon and Minions might forget their real characters.
lethe.examples:
The Storyteller secretly decides to use the Lethe. The Imp, the Baron and the Poisoner all think they are good characters. Because of the Baron's ability, there are 2 more Outsiders than the default. Each night, the Storyteller uses the Imp's and the Poisoner's abilities for them. On the fourth day, the Imp, the Baron and the Poisoner have all died by execution, and the Storyteller announces that all players win together.

The Storyteller secretly decides not to use the Lethe. The game proceeds normally; the Lethe has no effect on it.
lethe.tips:
If you get a good character: whether the Lethe is in use makes little difference to your goal, which is always to find and execute suspicious evil players.

If you get a good character and you suspect your ability isn't working properly, you can ask to be executed, since you may be an evil player affected by the Lethe.

If you get a Minion or Demon character, the Lethe is certainly not in use this game. But you can use that to invent reasoning that the Lethe is in use, and even trick good into executing themselves, helping you win.
lethe.bluffing:
Early in the game, the Storyteller should make things look as much like a normal game as possible.

If the Lethe is exposed, never mind: carry on as normal and wait for the players to execute all the evil players.

If the players are making no progress at all, you can "help" them within the rules — for example, give poisoned or drunk players, or players who think they are the Demon or Minions, fairly "outlandish" information, or use the Demon's ability at night to kill an evil player. Whatever you do, you must follow the rules: nothing you do may break the rules of the game.

lucky_star.ability: The player who draws this token gets some "perks" and draws another token. [This token is added to the bag as an extra]
lucky_star.summary: The player who draws the Lucky Star gets some good luck.
lucky_star.examples:
The Storyteller announces that whoever draws the Lucky Star plays for free today. Sam draws the Lucky Star, hands it to the Storyteller, then draws again and gets the Fortune Teller.

The Storyteller announces that whoever draws the Lucky Star gets a small gift the Storyteller has prepared. Sam draws the Lucky Star, hands it to the Storyteller, then draws again and gets the Fortune Teller. Sam gets the gift.

The Storyteller announces that whoever draws the Lucky Star gets the character they want in the next game. Sam draws the Lucky Star, hands it to the Storyteller, then draws again and gets the Fortune Teller. In the next game, Sam gets the Tinker, which they wanted to play.

hells_roulette.ability: After nominating, a player rolls a six-sided die: if that number has already been rolled, they die, and all rolled dice are removed.
hells_roulette.summary: A player who nominates takes on a big risk of dying.
hells_roulette.examples:
On the first day, the Fortune Teller nominates and rolls a 1. The Saint nominates and rolls a 1, so the Saint dies. Both dice are removed.

On the first day, the Fortune Teller nominates and rolls a 1. The Saint nominates and rolls a 6. The Butler nominates and rolls a 5. The Baron nominates and rolls a 1, so the Baron dies. All 4 dice are removed.

With only one six-sided die, the Storyteller records the number each nominating player rolls. If a roll repeats a recorded number, the nominating player dies and the record is cleared.
